datasets.label: open-pulse.rete — EPFL/SDSC research-software knowledge graph (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The Open-Pulse graph of research software in and around EPFL and the Swiss Data Science Center. 40,574 crawled GitHub entities — 31,787 repositories (schema:SoftwareSourceCode), 7,819 people (schema:Person) and 968 organizations (org:Organization) — plus the edges between them: who contributed to what (pulse:Contribution, person→repo, with commit counts and first/last dates), who is affiliated with which institution (org:Membership, person→org), which org owns which repo (pulse:ownedBy), and the scholarly articles repositories cite (schema:ScholarlyArticle). Built by the Open-Pulse git-metadata-extractor and modelled with the Open-Pulse ontology: schema.org + the W3C Organization & Time vocabularies + the project's pulse: terms, with raw GitHub facts (stars, forks, primary language, topics, timestamps) under the gme: namespace and institutions reconciled to ROR (country, type). People carry both their GitHub handle and, where reconciled, an ORCID. 3.70 M triples, a types pyramid and embedded Dataset Card. Per source_url the latest complete extraction is kept; the extractor's double-prefixed GitHub IRIs are normalized so repos join their owning org, and institution country is flattened from ROR. scripts/open-pulse/*.py → rete build --pyramid-algo types --card. Remote-lazy on Cloudflare R2.
datasets.license: GitHub public metadata (facts); Open-Pulse ontology © SDSC-ORDES

examples.title: What's in the graph
examples.tip:
The six entity types of the Open-Pulse model and how many of each: repositories (schema:SoftwareSourceCode), people (schema:Person), organizations (org:Organization), plus the pulse:Contribution and org:Membership edges and the schema:ScholarlyArticle citations.
Open the Schema tab to see the same breakdown as a type pyramid.

examples.title: ⭐ Most-starred repositories
examples.tip:
The highest-starred repositories in the crawl, with their primary language — a mix of EPFL/SDSC projects and the big open-source libraries they build on.
Stars come from pulse:githubRepoStars; the OPTIONAL keeps repos that have no detected language.

examples.title: 🏛 Organizations with the most repositories
examples.tip:
Which GitHub organizations own the most crawled repositories — EPFL labs and course orgs (ADA, EPFL-SI, LASA …) rise to the top.
pulse:ownedBy links a repo to its owning org; an org can carry more than one schema:name, so we SAMPLE one.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX pulse: <https://open-pulse.epfl.ch/ontology#>
PREFIX org: <http://www.w3.org/ns/org#>
SELECT ?org (SAMPLE(?nm) AS ?name) (COUNT(?repo) AS ?repos) WHERE {
  ?repo a schema:SoftwareSourceCode ; pulse:ownedBy ?org .
  ?org a org:Organization ; schema:name ?nm .
} GROUP BY ?org ORDER BY DESC(?repos) LIMIT 40

examples.title: 👥 Who built CEBRA
examples.tip:
The contributors to CEBRA (the Mathis Lab / AdaptiveMotorControlLab neural-embedding library) ranked by commit count. Each row is a pulse:Contribution edge from a person to the repo, carrying pulse:contributionCount.
Some contributors are identified by ORCID, others by GitHub handle; swap the repo IRI for any repository.

examples.title: 🌍 Research software by institution country
examples.tip:
Count repositories by the country of their owning organization's parent institution — a repo's GitHub org links to a ROR institution (org:unitOf) that carries gme:ror_country. Switzerland dominates, as you'd expect for an EPFL/SDSC crawl.
The country was flattened from ROR's nested country object during the build.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX pulse: <https://open-pulse.epfl.ch/ontology#>
PREFIX org: <http://www.w3.org/ns/org#>
PREFIX gme: <https://openpulse.science/git-metadata-extractor#>
SELECT ?country (COUNT(DISTINCT ?repo) AS ?repos) WHERE {
  ?repo a schema:SoftwareSourceCode ; pulse:ownedBy ?ghorg .
  ?ghorg org:unitOf ?ror .
  ?ror gme:ror_country ?country .
} GROUP BY ?country ORDER BY DESC(?repos) LIMIT 20

examples.title: 🏛 EPFL research software (most-starred first)
examples.tip:
All software owned by an EPFL lab, most-starred first — so the top row is EPFL's flagship repo (Stable-Video-Infinity, from the VITA lab). EPFL's ROR institution is ror.org/02s376052; a repo's GitHub org (the lab) links to it via org:unitOf, and gme:primary_language gives the language.
Swap the ROR IRI for any institution (e.g. ETH Zürich) to retarget the whole query.

examples.title: 🍴 Forks (dependents) of EPFL software
examples.tip:
Software downstream of EPFL: every repo that is a fork of an EPFL-owned repo, with the EPFL original it derives from. NOTE — this graph has no package-dependency edge (that lived in the raw crawler graphs, not the ontology metadata), so 'dependents' here means the fork relation the model does capture, pulse:isForkOf.
EPFL-owned = its GitHub org is org:unitOf the EPFL ROR (ror.org/02s376052).

examples.title: 🏆 EPFL labs ranked by total stars
examples.tip:
Which EPFL labs produce the most-starred software: every GitHub org that is org:unitOf the EPFL ROR, ranked by the combined stars of all its repositories — VITA, CVLAB, epfml and DEDIS lead.
?org is the lab's GitHub org IRI; ?repos counts its repositories in the crawl.

examples.title: 👥 EPFL-affiliated developers
examples.tip:
People with an org:Membership to EPFL (the ROR institution ror.org/02s376052), ranked by how many repositories they own — most are reconciled to an ORCID, so ?person is often the ORCID IRI itself.
The membership carries time:hasBeginning/hasEnd if you want to filter by affiliation dates.

examples.title: 🔎 Everything about one repository (gimie)
examples.tip:
All data associated with a single repository — here sdsc-ordes/gimie (SDSC's Git-metadata extractor, the tool behind this graph). The 'out' rows are the repo's own facts (stars, language, license, dates, owner, disciplines, package registries…); the 'in' rows are everything that points AT it — each pulse:Contribution edge from a contributor, its owning org (pulse:owns), and any fork (pulse:isForkOf).
Swap the IRI for <https://github.com/DeepLabCut/DeepLabCut> or any repository to describe it.

datasets.label: scholar.rete - synthetic scholarly world
datasets.description: 250 papers, 137 authors, 36 venues from scripts/synth_graph.py (seed 42): power-law citations, field communities, Zipfian venues, and typed literals.

examples.title: One query, all three engines (Whole · Progressive · Community)
examples.tip: The same answer — 6,954 triples — under every Strategy. Switch the dropdown and watch the machinery change: Whole index scans the full SPO index; Progressive answers exactly from the pyramid summary in ~3 small range reads, never touching the triple index; Split by community sums 13 per-community partials. Identical result, three different engines.
examples.sparql: SELECT (COUNT(*) AS ?triples) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o }

examples.title: Predicate totals
examples.tip: Progressive strategy: exact per-predicate counts straight from the pyramid summary — the triple index is skipped. Also correct under Whole index and Split by community.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p (COUNT(*) AS ?triples) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o } GROUP BY ?p

examples.title: Author profiles
examples.tip: Names, integer-typed h-index values, and affiliations, highest h-index first.

examples.title: High-novelty papers
examples.tip: FILTER over an xsd:double literal (noveltyScore is log-normal, so the tail is short).

examples.title: High-novelty, split by community
examples.tip: The split strategy: subject stars evaluate per pyramid community, joins recombine the partials globally, FILTER/ORDER BY semantics intact — identical rows to the whole-index run.

examples.title: Citation closure (Whole index only)
examples.tip: Transitive cito:cites+ from one recent paper reaches 73 papers (citations only point backwards in time). A property path needs the Whole index: Progressive can't serve it from the summary, and Split by community refuses it (a pure path has nothing to split).
examples.sparql:
PREFIX cito: <http://purl.org/spar/cito/>
SELECT DISTINCT ?reached WHERE { <http://ex/paper/245> cito:cites+ ?reached }

examples.title: Most-cited papers
examples.tip: Counts incoming cito:cites per paper and ranks them, exposing the preferential-attachment power law: a handful of papers soak up most of the citations while the long tail gets almost none.

examples.title: Papers per field
examples.tip: Groups papers by ex:hasField and counts each, giving a Zipfian size distribution: genomics dominates the corpus while the remaining fields thin out quickly down the tail.

examples.title: Authors above the mean h-index
examples.tip: A subquery computes the average h-index in its own scope; the outer query keeps only authors beating it. Nested SELECT support makes this one query.

examples.title: Novelty tiers (IF)
examples.tip: Nested IF() buckets each paper's xsd:double novelty score into high / medium / low — a BIND the rest of the query can see.

examples.title: Title fingerprints (SHA-256)
examples.tip: SHA256 (and MD5 / SHA1 / SHA384 / SHA512) plus STRLEN are part of the SPARQL 1.1 function library — a content hash of each title and its length.

examples.title: Everything but citations
examples.tip: A negated property set !(cito:cites) walks one step over every predicate except citation edges — all the non-citation facts of one paper.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX cito: <http://purl.org/spar/cito/>
SELECT ?o WHERE { <http://ex/paper/15> !(cito:cites) ?o }

examples.title: Coauthor ego network
examples.tip: CONSTRUCTs a two-hop coauthorship ego network around author/105, the busiest hub: its direct coauthors (the first UNION branch) plus their coauthors (the second), drawn as a graph.

shacl_shapes.title: Paper integrity
shacl_shapes.tip: Every paper needs exactly one title, a venue, and a double-typed novelty score - the clean graph conforms.

shacl_shapes.title: Single keyword only
shacl_shapes.tip: Intentional violation: papers carry 2-5 keywords by design, so maxCount 1 flags all 240 of them.

shacl_shapes.title: Authors carry an ORCID + h-index
shacl_shapes.tip: Every ex:Person should declare an ORCID and an h-index. The clean graph conforms.

shacl_shapes.title: Journals carry an ISSN
shacl_shapes.tip: Every ex:Journal should declare an ISSN. The clean graph conforms.

datasets.label: wikidata-1GB.rete - a real 1 GB Wikidata graph (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: A real ~1.04 GB slice of Wikidata, queried entirely in the browser over HTTP range requests - the point is that a GIGABYTE-scale knowledge graph stays interactive because a selective SPARQL query only faults in the bytes it needs (a typical query reads ~40 MB of the 1.04 GB, never the whole file). Holds both PLACES (e.g. wd:Q100001 Bemelen, with multilingual schema:description) and PEOPLE (wd:Q5 humans with wdt:P106 occupation, wdt:P569 birth date, wdt:P737 influenced-by). Entity/property IRIs stay as wikidata.org/{entity,prop/direct}/* so nodes round-trip to live Wikidata. Use bound subjects/objects and occupation intersections for snappy reads; avoid full scans. CC0 (Wikidata). See also the dedicated 100 MB / 1 GB explorer.

examples.title: All facts about an entity
examples.tip: A bound subject is the most selective query shape: SPO routing jumps straight to the tiles holding Bemelen (entity Q100001, a small Dutch village), so the reader fetches only a few HTTP ranges of the whole file - never a scan. Its coordinate comes back as a geo:wktLiteral, the datatype reconstructed during the parquet -> rete build.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p ?o WHERE { <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/Q100001> ?p ?o }

examples.title: Labels of an entity, across languages
examples.tip: Bound subject + bound predicate (rdfs:label) is the tightest shape of all - it touches only the label tiles for Bemelen (Q100001), a handful of bytes. The second column is each label's language tag (LANG), so you can read the same entity named across dozens of languages instead of a single opaque row.

examples.title: Find a thing by its name
examples.tip: The inverse of looking up by Q-id - start from a human string. CONTAINS scans rdfs:label for the text you type (here 'bemelen', matching the village Q100001) and returns each entity paired with its name. A plain substring search faults more label tiles than a bound lookup; for big graphs rete can build an optional TEXT_INDEX so this becomes a few range reads instead of a scan.

examples.title: Coordinates of a place
examples.tip: wdt:P625 is Wikidata's 'coordinate location' property. For Bemelen (Q100001) it returns a single geo:wktLiteral point - the WKT datatype recovered during the parquet -> rete conversion, so it round-trips as proper GeoSPARQL rather than an opaque string.

examples.title: Subclasses of a class (with names)
examples.tip: A reverse bound-object lookup: every class that declares wdt:P279 (subclass of) -> Q515, the entity for 'city'. The bound object routes to just the POS tiles for that one edge, and the OPTIONAL rdfs:label join adds an English-name column so you read 'town, capital, seaport, ...' instead of bare Q-ids.

examples.title: Physicists who are also philosophers (in 1 GB)
examples.tip: The occupation intersection (people who are both wdt:P106 physicist Q169470 and philosopher Q4964182) on the lazy 1 GB file. Optimised shape: the intersection runs in a subquery with LIMIT, so the name, birth year (wdt:P569) and English description (schema:description) are resolved for only the ~25 people that pass - not the thousands in each occupation. Reading both whole occupation sets to intersect them is still the heavy part; enable Settings -> Range cache so a re-run is near-instant.

examples.title: Painters who are also writers
examples.tip: Another occupation intersection - people who are both wdt:P106 painter (Q1028181) and writer (Q36180), polymaths like William Blake. The remote-aware join scans both occupation sets in bulk and intersects them, then resolves the name and birth year for the handful that pass.

examples.title: Physicists born before 1900
examples.tip: People by year: seed on a selective occupation (physicists, wdt:P106 Q169470), then keep those whose birth year - YEAR(wdt:P569) - is before 1900. Seeding on the occupation first means only physicists' birth dates are read, never the whole date-of-birth predicate. Oldest first.

examples.title: People born in Paris
examples.tip: City of birth: a bound object on wdt:P19 (place of birth) -> Q90 (Paris) routes straight to the people born there - a selective lazy read - then resolves each one's name, birth year and occupation.

examples.title: Painters born in Paris
examples.tip: Occupation + city of birth: painters (wdt:P106 Q1028181) who were also born in Paris (wdt:P19 Q90). A double-bound intersection the remote-aware join handles by scanning both sets and intersecting, with each painter's birth year.

examples.title: Composers born in the 1700s
examples.tip: People by era: seed on composers (wdt:P106 Q36834), then keep those born in the 18th century - 1700 <= YEAR(wdt:P569) < 1800 - Bach, Mozart, Haydn and contemporaries. Only composers' birth dates are read, oldest first.

examples.title: Writers and their country of citizenship
examples.tip: Seed on a selective occupation (writers, wdt:P106 Q36180), then resolve each one's country of citizenship (wdt:P27) and birth year. Three readable columns from one occupation seed - a few range reads of the 1 GB file.

examples.title: Build a small graph (export as TTL / JSON-LD)
examples.tip: A CONSTRUCT builds a NEW RDF graph - here a card for each scientist-philosopher (label, description, image). Because it produces triples, you can switch Output to TTL or JSON-LD to read and copy the serialization. (TTL / JSON-LD write triples, so they only apply to CONSTRUCT or DESCRIBE - a SELECT returns a table, not a graph.)

shacl_shapes.title: People with a job have a birth date
shacl_shapes.tip: Note: SHACL validates the whole graph in memory, which isn't viable at 1 GB in the browser — run these on the wikidata-100MB twin (same shapes, same vocab) or Cache remote. Every person with an occupation should record a date of birth.

shacl_shapes.title: People with a job have a citizenship
shacl_shapes.tip: Best run on the wikidata-100MB twin (1 GB can't be materialized for SHACL). Every person with an occupation should record a country of citizenship.

shacl_shapes.title: People with a job have a place of birth
shacl_shapes.tip: Best run on the wikidata-100MB twin. Every person with an occupation should record a place of birth.

shacl_shapes.title: People with a birthplace are labelled
shacl_shapes.tip: Best run on the wikidata-100MB twin. Every person who records a place of birth should also carry a label.

datasets.label: wikidata with Zenodo DOI (1 GB) - citable source, stable R2 delivery
datasets.description: The same ~1.49 GB Wikidata graph deposited as the citable Zenodo record 21168821 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21168821), served here as its stable-format R2 twin for browser range queries. The deposited pre-1.0 artifact remains the provenance record; this release copy carries stable format generation 1 and browser-visible Content-Range. A selective query faults ~27 MB rather than downloading the whole file. CC0 (Wikidata).

examples.title: Everything about Plato
examples.tip: A bound subject is the most selective shape: SPO routing jumps straight to the tiles holding wd:Q859, so the reader fetches only a few HTTP ranges - from the Zenodo DOI, never a scan of the 1.5 GB.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p ?o WHERE { <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/Q859> ?p ?o }

examples.title: 20 typed entities (instance-of)
examples.tip: A cheap bound-predicate scan over a gigabyte hosted on Zenodo. Wikidata types entities with wdt:P31 (instance of), not rdf:type; reads a few MB, not the whole file.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?s ?type WHERE { ?s <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/P31> ?type } LIMIT 20

examples.title: Physicists who were also philosophers
examples.tip: Occupation intersection: P106 = physicist (Q169470) AND philosopher (Q4964182), with an English label. A selective join, every byte range-fetched from the Zenodo record.

examples.title: Most common occupations
examples.tip: GROUP BY + COUNT over the P106 predicate. Aggregates touch more tiles than a bound query but still only the occupation slices - a good stress test of HTTP range-reads against Zenodo.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX wdt: <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/>
SELECT ?occ (COUNT(?p) AS ?n) WHERE {
  ?p wdt:P106 ?occ
}
GROUP BY ?occ
ORDER BY DESC(?n)
LIMIT 15

datasets.label: wikidata-ontology.rete — every Wikidata class: the ontology without the instances (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The complete class ontology of Wikidata, extracted from the full truthy dump — the file Wikidata itself never publishes. All 4,420,121 classes (every item that is a wdt:P279 subject or object, or the target of any of the 120.8M wdt:P31 statements) with their FULL multilingual stars — labels, aliases and descriptions in every language (4.27M carry English labels) plus every other truthy statement whose subject is a class — the 5,144,945-edge subclass hierarchy, and all ~13k property entities. wdt:P279 is dual-emitted as rdfs:subClassOf and wdt:P31 as rdf:type, so the types pyramid, plain SPARQL tooling and reasoning work out of the box alongside Wikidata-native wdt: queries. Each of the 109,558 instantiated classes carries rete:instanceCount — its direct-instance census in the full ~8B-statement dump (scholarly article 45.2M, human 12.7M, taxon 3.8M, star 3.3M…), so you can weigh any branch of the taxonomy without touching a single instance. GeoSPARQL on board: place-anchored classes carry wdt:P625 geo:wktLiteral points (off-world geometries — lakes on Mars — carry a <wd:Q111> CRS prefix, which is valid GeoSPARQL). A full-text index covers all labels. 185.5M triples / 53.7M terms in 2.18 GB, remote-lazy over HTTP range on Cloudflare R2, with the whole metadata bundle beside it: wikidata-taxonomy.ttl (a 13.9M-statement compact Turtle — class + English label + subClassOf + census — for Protégé/reasoners), croissant.json (MLCommons Croissant 1.0), JSON Schemas, and the classes / class_counts / p279 Parquet side-tables. Built by scripts/wikidata_ontology_to_nt.py (two DuckDB passes over the piebro/wikidata-extraction Parquet of the official truthy dump, authoritative property datatypes) → rete build --pyramid-algo types --card --text-index. CC0 (Wikidata).

examples.title: 🏛️ Subclasses of building, weighed by census
examples.tip:
wd:Q41176 is 'building' — these are its direct subclasses ranked by how many instances each has in the FULL ~8B-statement dump (rete:instanceCount, precomputed from all 120.8M wdt:P31 rows): Shinto shrine (30,332) beats residential building (27,497) and palace (16,357).
Swap Q41176 for any class IRI to weigh a different branch of the taxonomy without ever touching an instance.

examples.title: 📊 The census of Wikidata: biggest classes and their parents
examples.tip:
Every instantiated class ranked by its direct-instance count in full Wikidata: scholarly article (45.2M) dwarfs human (12.7M), taxon (3.8M) and star (3.3M).
A class repeats once per parent — scholarly article genuinely has four superclasses (magazine article, research, scientific literature, scientific publication); that is honest multi-inheritance, not duplication.

examples.title: 🏰 Everything a castle is (P279+ ancestors)
examples.tip:
wdt:P279+ walks the subclass hierarchy transitively upward from castle (wd:Q23413): fortification, military installation, venue, building… all the way to abstract roots — each ancestor with its English description and census.
The transitive path runs entirely in the browser over HTTP range reads; only the tiles along the chain are fetched.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX wd: <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/>
PREFIX wdt: <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX rete: <https://w3id.org/rete/>
SELECT ?ancestor ?name ?description ?instances WHERE {
  wd:Q23413 wdt:P279+ ?ancestor .
  ?ancestor rdfs:label ?name . FILTER(lang(?name) = "en")
  ?ancestor schema:description ?description . FILTER(lang(?description) = "en")
  OPTIONAL { ?ancestor rete:instanceCount ?instances }
}
LIMIT 60

examples.title: 🗺️ Classes anchored to a place
examples.tip:
Some classes are geographic one-offs — a recurring race, court or festival is the class, its editions are the instances, and the class itself sits at a place (the Grand National at Aintree, the US Open at Flushing Meadows). wdt:P625 values are GeoSPARQL wktLiterals — switch Output → Map to see them.
STRSTARTS keeps plain Earth points: the dump also holds unknown-coordinate hashes and off-world geometries (lakes on Mars carry a <wd:Q111> CRS prefix — valid GeoSPARQL, but not for this basemap). The query streams and stops at 50, so it stays fast over HTTP range reads.

examples.title: 🔭 The observatory family tree (P279+ descendants)
examples.tip:
The mirror of the castle query: wd:Q1254933 is 'astronomical observatory', and wdt:P279+ with the BOUND endpoint as the object walks the subclass tree DOWNWARD — space observatory, airborne observatory, radio observatory… each with its description and census.
Swap Q1254933 for any class IRI (find one via its rdfs:label) to unfold a different branch of the 5.1M-edge taxonomy.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX wd: <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/>
PREFIX wdt: <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX rete: <https://w3id.org/rete/>
SELECT ?sub ?name ?description ?instances WHERE {
  ?sub wdt:P279+ wd:Q1254933 .
  ?sub rdfs:label ?name . FILTER(lang(?name) = "en")
  ?sub schema:description ?description . FILTER(lang(?description) = "en")
  OPTIONAL { ?sub rete:instanceCount ?instances }
}
LIMIT 60

datasets.label: scholar-noisy.rete - same world, 25% noise
datasets.description: The same generator at --noise 0.25: rewired citations (incl. temporal violations), missing ORCIDs and ISSNs, and whitespace-mangled titles - for SHACL and data-quality demos.

examples.title: Predicate totals
examples.tip: Progressive strategy: exact per-predicate counts read straight from the pyramid summary in a few small range reads, so the triple index is never touched. The numbers are identical under the Whole-index strategy.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p (COUNT(*) AS ?triples) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o } GROUP BY ?p

examples.title: Mangled titles
examples.tip: REGEX(?title, "^  ") matches titles that start with stray leading whitespace - the formatting mess the noise knob injected into 20 of them - so it surfaces exactly those dirty records.

examples.title: Authors missing ORCID
examples.tip: FILTER NOT EXISTS keeps only ex:Person records that have no ex:orcid triple at all - the 16 authors whose ORCID the noise knob stripped out. A classic data-completeness check.

examples.title: Noise-inflated closure
examples.tip: The same seed paper reaches 16 papers in the clean graph - rewired citations inflate it to 228 here.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX cito: <http://purl.org/spar/cito/>
SELECT DISTINCT ?reached WHERE { <http://ex/paper/249> cito:cites+ ?reached }

examples.title: Temporal violations
examples.tip: Papers citing later-dated papers - impossible without noise; 298 of them here.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX cito: <http://purl.org/spar/cito/>
PREFIX dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/>
SELECT (COUNT(*) AS ?violations) WHERE {
  ?citing cito:cites ?cited .
  ?citing dct:date ?d1 .
  ?cited dct:date ?d2 .
  FILTER(STR(?d2) > STR(?d1))
}

examples.title: Cross-field citation pairs
examples.tip: Citations that jump fields are mostly noise rewires; the clean graph keeps them rare.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX ex: <http://ex/>
PREFIX cito: <http://purl.org/spar/cito/>
SELECT ?from ?to (COUNT(*) AS ?n) WHERE {
  ?a cito:cites ?b .
  ?a ex:hasField ?from .
  ?b ex:hasField ?to .
  FILTER(?from != ?to)
} GROUP BY ?from ?to ORDER BY DESC(?n) LIMIT 15

examples.title: Cross-field cites from genomics
examples.tip: CONSTRUCTs the noise as a graph: genomics papers (ex:hasField genomics) whose citations land in some other field. Real corpora rarely cross fields, so these edges are mostly the noise knob's rewires.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX ex: <http://ex/>
PREFIX cito: <http://purl.org/spar/cito/>
CONSTRUCT { ?a ex:crossFieldCite ?b } WHERE {
  ?a cito:cites ?b .
  ?a ex:hasField <http://ex/field/genomics> .
  ?b ex:hasField ?other .
  FILTER(?other != <http://ex/field/genomics>)
}

shacl_shapes.title: Author completeness
shacl_shapes.tip: The noise knob dropped ORCIDs and h-indexes - 27 violations here; the clean graph conforms.

shacl_shapes.title: Journals need an ISSN
shacl_shapes.tip: Four journals lost their ISSN to the noise knob.

shacl_shapes.title: Papers are titled and placed
shacl_shapes.tip: Every ex:Paper should carry exactly one title and a venue.

shacl_shapes.title: Conferences are named
shacl_shapes.tip: Every ex:Conference should carry an ex:name.

datasets.label: causal.rete - cardiometabolic causal model (confounders, mediators, colliders, loops)
datasets.description: A cardiometabolic causal model: ~30 typed factors (risk factors, conditions, diseases, symptoms, outcomes, treatments) wired by a transitive :causes relation, plus a protective :reduces relation. Built so the Query examples discover causal structure - confounders (forks), mediators (chains), colliders (common effects), feedback loops (?x :causes+ ?x), and exogenous root causes. The SHACL examples check data quality (three planted defects). And the Coherence tab still proves the schema defect: :Relapsed is a subclass of two owl:disjointWith classes (HealthyState, DiseaseState) so it is UNSATISFIABLE, and patient :p is typed as both states. ~170 triples.

examples.title: What's in the model

examples.title: Confounders (a common cause of two factors)

examples.title: Colliders (two causes, one effect)

examples.title: How obesity leads to diabetes (mediators)

examples.title: Exogenous root causes
examples.tip: Factors that cause something but that nothing in the model causes - the entry points for prevention. FILTER NOT EXISTS asks for no incoming ex:causes edge.

datasets.label: causalgraph.rete - causal graphs in knowledge graphs (Fraunhofer IWU ontology + example, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The causalgraph ontology (github.com/causalgraph/causalgraph, MIT - a Python package for modelling, persisting and visualising causal graphs as RDF) brought to rete: the full OWL schema (converted from OWL/XML with owlready2) PLUS an authored example causal model. The ONTOLOGY (TBox) defines how a causal graph is represented: a CausalGraph is made of CausalNodes (each an Event, State or Variable, split by origin into Human-input vs Machine) and CausalEdges; every CausalEdge reifies a cause→effect link carrying hasConfidence (0-1), hasTimeLag (the delay before the effect), and a Creator provenance - a Human_Creator (domain knowledge) or a Machine_Creator / LearningAlgorithm_Creator (a causal-discovery run). Class definitions come straight from the OWL (rdfs:comment). The EXAMPLE (ABox, scripts/causalgraph_example.py) is a faithful Industry-4.0 causal graph - INJECTION-MOULDING quality: operator setpoint → injection pressure → mould fill → short-shot/warpage, melt temperature → burn marks, etc., with realistic confidences + time-lags, some edges asserted by the process engineer and others 'discovered' by a PCMCI run. 315 triples (ontology + example), embedded. Explore the schema (Schema view), traverse cause→effect, rank by confidence, or split links by who asserted them. MIT (causalgraph / Fraunhofer IWU).

examples.title: The causal model (cause → effect, confidence, lag)
examples.tip: Every CausalEdge reifies a cause→effect link carrying hasConfidence (0-1: how sure the mechanism is) and hasTimeLag (seconds until the effect shows). The injection-moulding model, ranked by confidence: operator setpoint → injection pressure (0.98, +0s), pressure → mould fill (0.92, +2s), cooling time → warpage (0.81, +30s)...

examples.title: What causes a defect?
examples.tip: The direct causes of the short-shot defect: insufficient injection pressure (0.80) and incomplete mould fill (0.65). Edges are REIFIED, so you walk node <- edge(hasEffect) and edge(hasCause) -> node. Trace further back (pressure <- setpoint) for the whole chain.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX cg: <http://iwu.fraunhofer.de/causalgraph#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?cause ?confidence WHERE {
  ?effect rdfs:label "Short-shot defect" .
  ?e cg:hasEffect ?effect ; cg:hasCause ?c ; cg:hasConfidence ?confidence .
  ?c rdfs:label ?cause .
} ORDER BY DESC(?confidence)

examples.title: Downstream effects of injection pressure
examples.tip: Everything injection pressure directly causes - mould fill (0.92, +2s), the short-shot defect (0.80, +2s) and part warpage (0.60, +25s). The time-lags reveal how long after a pressure change each effect appears.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX cg: <http://iwu.fraunhofer.de/causalgraph#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?effect ?confidence ?timeLag WHERE {
  ?cause rdfs:label "Injection pressure" .
  ?e cg:hasCause ?cause ; cg:hasEffect ?f ; cg:hasConfidence ?confidence ; cg:hasTimeLag ?timeLag .
  ?f rdfs:label ?effect .
} ORDER BY DESC(?confidence)

examples.title: Human knowledge vs algorithm-discovered
examples.tip: causalgraph records WHERE each edge came from (hasCreator). Some links were ASSERTED by the process engineer (press physics - domain knowledge); others were DISCOVERED by a PCMCI causal-discovery run on the data. Provenance is first-class - you can trust, filter or audit the model by who claimed each edge.

examples.title: The ontology: classes & definitions
examples.tip: The causalgraph ontology itself (the TBox, shipped in the same file). A CausalNode is an Event, State or Variable (split Human-input vs Machine); a CausalEdge connects two nodes with a direction + confidence; a Creator is the human or machine that asserted an individual. Definitions are the OWL rdfs:comment, verbatim.

examples.title: The class hierarchy
examples.tip: The taxonomy via rdfs:subClassOf: Machine_Variable -> Variable -> CausalNode; LearningAlgorithm_Creator -> Machine_Creator -> Creator. The 'origin' axis (Human-input vs Machine) and the 'kind' axis (Event / State / Variable) together classify every causal node.

datasets.label: ontoneurolog.rete - a neuroimaging data-sharing ontology (OntoNeuroLOG v2.2, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: OntoNeuroLOG v2.2 - the application ontology of the NeuroLOG project (Temal, Dojat, Kassel & Gibaud, J. Biomed. Inform. 2008), which federated four French neuroscience centres (Grenoble, Rennes, Paris, Sophia Antipolis) to share MRI data across their heterogeneous databases. This is a SCHEMA (a TBox, no instance data): a DOLCE-grounded, multi-layer OWL-Lite ontology shipped as 35 RDF/XML modules and merged here into one graph. Its richest layer is a careful model of MR PHYSICS and ACQUISITION - an MR-protocol specifies the actions of an MR dataset acquisition; an MR-sequence specifies RF pulses, gradients and signal reading (spin-echo, gradient-echo, EPI...); classes like flip-angle, field-of-view, coil, 1H-nucleus and MR-image-contrast carry scholarly rdfs:comment definitions citing DICOM, Hornak and Boyle. Around it sit taxonomies of DATASETS (acquisition vs processing - the dataset-processing branch is a tree of neuroimaging pipeline operations: mesh generation, wavelet transformation, calibration-model estimation), MEDICAL-IMAGE files and formats, EXAMINATION SUBJECTS (human, sex, hemispheric dominance), STUDIES, software SERVICES, and clinical ASSESSMENT INSTRUMENTS (e.g. every item of the BDI-II Beck Depression Inventory). The DOLCE upper layer and an I&DA 'information & discourse acts' core give it its backbone of participant-role object properties (is-agent-of-at, has-for-function, generates, is-capable-to-perform) that wire actions, agents and artefacts together. 17,658 triples, 1,303 classes, 289 object properties, remote-lazy over HTTP range. Explore the schema (Schema view), read the MR definitions, or CONSTRUCT a subclass tree as a graph. Public download from the NeuroLOG namespace; explicit licence unstated - attribute B. Gibaud / IRISA-VISAGES and cite Temal et al. 2008. Merged from the 35 public OWL modules by scripts/ontoneurolog_to_nt.py. Pairs naturally with NIDM (the RDF Neuroimaging Data Model) for actual provenance instances.
datasets.license: Public download; licence unstated — attribute B. Gibaud / IRISA-VISAGES, cite Temal et al. 2008

examples.title: The shape of the ontology (classes per module)
examples.tip: OntoNeuroLOG is 35 OWL modules; this counts the owl:Class in each. The instruments-declaration module dominates (440 - every item of clinical scales like the BDI-II), then MR physics (mr-protocol 120, mr-sequence 46), the dataset taxonomies (dataset-processing 86, dataset 73) and the DOLCE 'particular' upper layer. A one-query map of where the modelling effort went.

examples.title: MR physics, defined
examples.tip: The heart of the ontology: the 111 classes of the mr-sequence and mr-protocol modules with their scholarly rdfs:comment definitions. An MR-protocol 'specifies the actions to perform an MR dataset acquisition'; flip-angle, field-of-view, coil and 1H-nucleus are each defined with citations to the DICOM standard, Hornak (2006) and Boyle et al. Read it like a referenced glossary of MRI.

examples.title: How the concepts connect (the grammar)
examples.tip: The ontology's grammar: every owl:ObjectProperty with its rdfs:domain and rdfs:range - what may link to what. This is the DOLCE / participant-role backbone - an agentive is-agent-of-at an action, a functional-entity has-for-function a function, an action generates an action - the relations that turn a class list into a model.

examples.title: The image-processing taxonomy (graph)
examples.tip: CONSTRUCT the rdfs:subClassOf tree of the dataset-processing module and render it as a node-and-arrow graph. These are neuroimaging pipeline operations - wavelet-transformation and unstructured-mesh-generation are kinds of dataset-transformation / mesh-generation; voxel-displacement-map-calculation is a calibration-model-estimation. The taxonomy a NeuroLOG processing service is classified against.

examples.title: Clinical assessment instruments (BDI-II)
examples.tip: Beyond imaging, OntoNeuroLOG models the clinical scales used in neuroscience studies. Here every item of the BDI-II (Beck Depression Inventory II) - agitation, changes-in-appetite, concentration-difficulty... - each a labelled owl:Class in the instruments-declaration module, the kind of psychometric variable a study records alongside the MRI.

datasets.label: nidm.rete - Neuroimaging Data Model: a real cohort + PROV provenance (federates with ontoneurolog)
datasets.description: NIDM (the Neuroimaging Data Model, INCF NIDASH / BIRN) - the RDF + W3C PROV standard for describing the neuroimaging data lifecycle - carrying a REAL cohort: OpenNeuro ds000030, the UCLA Consortium for Neuropsychiatric Phenomics. 272 subjects (nidm:AcquisitionObject / prov:Entity) each with ncit:age (21-50), ncit:gender and ncit:diagnosis across four groups - 130 CONTROL, 50 SCHZ (schizophrenia), 49 BIPOLAR, 43 ADHD - and full PROV provenance: every acquisition prov:wasGeneratedBy an activity and prov:wasAttributedTo an agent. Bundled with the OntoNeuroLOG v3.0 assessment-instrument taxonomy that NIDM reuses (assessment-instrument, questionnaire, behavioural-instrument, scale-item, numerical-score... each with a skos:definition). THE FEDERATION COMPANION to the ontoneurolog dataset: because NIDM adopted OntoNeuroLOG's instrument ontology (at v3.0, http://neurolog.unice.fr/...) while ontoneurolog holds it at v2.2 (irisa.fr/...), this file ships 45 owl:sameAs links bridging the two versions by shared concept - so a CROSS-SOURCE JOIN (add ontoneurolog as a second source) links each NIDM instrument to its OntoNeuroLOG definition and returns 29 concepts defined on both sides. The honest reading: OntoNeuroLOG is the schema (definitions), NIDM is the instances (a real studied cohort) - the two halves of the NeuroLOG vision. 3,153 triples, remote-lazy over HTTP range. NIDM specs are an open community standard (INCF NIDASH, no explicit licence file); the ds000030 phenotype data derives from the OpenNeuro CC0 dataset (UCLA CNP). Built by scripts/nidm_to_nt.py from github.com/incf-nidash/nidm-specs. Extendable with NIDM-Results (FSL/SPM brain-mapping statistics) - future work.

examples.title: The cohort: subjects by diagnosis
examples.tip: The real ds000030 cohort (UCLA Consortium for Neuropsychiatric Phenomics), grouped by ncit:diagnosis: 130 healthy CONTROL, 50 SCHZ (schizophrenia), 49 BIPOLAR, 43 ADHD - 272 subjects in all. Each is a nidm:AcquisitionObject, the entity a scan produced.

examples.title: Mean age per diagnosis group
examples.tip: Age (ncit:age, 21-50 across the cohort) averaged within each diagnostic group. A one-line demographic profile of ds000030 - the kind of summary you would compute before a group analysis; the controls skew slightly younger than the clinical groups.

examples.title: PROV: how each scan was produced
examples.tip: NIDM's core is W3C PROV. Every acquisition records its provenance: prov:wasGeneratedBy the activity that produced it and prov:wasAttributedTo the agent responsible. This is the whole point of NIDM - the data carries where it came from, machine-readably.

examples.title: OntoNeuroLOG instruments, reused by NIDM
examples.tip: NIDM-Experiment doesn't reinvent psychometrics - it REUSES OntoNeuroLOG's assessment-instrument taxonomy (at v3.0). Here those instrument concepts (assessment-instrument, questionnaire, behavioural-instrument, scale-item, numerical-score...) with their skos:definition, shipped inside this file. The bridge to the ontoneurolog dataset (see the next, federated, example).
examples.sparql:
PREFIX owl: <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
SELECT ?instrument ?definition WHERE {
  ?c a owl:Class ; skos:definition ?definition .
  FILTER(STRSTARTS(STR(?c), "http://neurolog.unice.fr/ontoneurolog/v3.0/instrument.owl#"))
  BIND(STRAFTER(STR(?c), "#") AS ?instrument)
} ORDER BY ?instrument

examples.title: ★ Cross-source: NIDM instruments × OntoNeuroLOG definitions
examples.tip: The real federation: ONE query split across TWO datasets and JOINED. NIDM adopted OntoNeuroLOG's instrument ontology at v3.0 (neurolog.unice.fr) while the ontoneurolog dataset holds it at v2.2 (irisa.fr); this file ships owl:sameAs links bridging the two. The playground routes ?v3 owl:sameAs ?v2 + ?v3 skos:definition to NIDM and ?v2 rdfs:comment to ontoneurolog (the only source with rdfs:comment), meeting on the shared ?v2 - so each concept (the ?v2 IRI names it, e.g. .../questionnaire) shows BOTH definitions, v2.2 and v3.0, both CDISC-sourced. 29 concepts defined on both sides; ontoneurolog is pre-added as a second source (see the Sources strip).
examples.sparql:
PREFIX owl: <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
SELECT ?v2 ?ontoneurologDef ?nidmDef WHERE {
  ?v3 owl:sameAs ?v2 .
  ?v3 skos:definition ?nidmDef .
  ?v2 rdfs:comment ?ontoneurologDef .
}

datasets.label: mira-wikidata.rete - MIrA↔Wikidata mappings (SSSOM linkset, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: A MAPPING LINKSET, not a dataset: the 13 skos:exactMatch links reconciling MIrA's manuscript-culture entities (people, texts) to Wikidata - re-expressed from MIrA's owl:sameAs and shared the way the community does it, via SSSOM (Simple Standard for Sharing Ontological Mappings). Each link carries provenance as an owl:Axiom reification: sssom:mapping_justification (semapv:ManualMappingCuration), sssom:confidence, sssom:subject_label; the set itself is a void:Linkset / sssom:MappingSet with license, creator and date. The point: mappings are a CLAIM, not a fact, so they live in their OWN small, citable, queryable artifact - decoupled from both datasets - and federate IN to bridge them. See the MIrA example 'Same join, but via a shareable mapping linkset': the cross-source join routes ?p skos:exactMatch ?wd through THIS file, the entity label through MIrA, and the facts through live Wikidata. 125 triples, embedded. Built by scripts/mira_sssom.py (TSV companion: mira-wikidata.sssom.tsv). CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (MIrA).

examples.title: The mappings
examples.tip: The whole linkset: every MIrA entity reconciled to Wikidata as skos:exactMatch - 13 manual mappings (people + texts): Eriugena -> Q184500, Isidore -> Q166876, the Pauline Epistles -> Q265283... This is the shareable bridge; ?wikidata renders as a clickable link.

examples.title: A mapping with its SSSOM provenance
examples.tip: A mapping is a CLAIM, not a fact - so SSSOM records who/how/how-sure. Each link is reified as an owl:Axiom carrying sssom:mapping_justification (semapv:ManualMappingCuration = a human curated it), sssom:confidence (1.0) and the subject_label. datasets.label: mira.rete - early Irish manuscripts (MIrA, Wikidata-aligned, IIIF, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: MIrA - Manuscripts with Irish Associations (Pádraic Moran, University of Galway): a catalogue of c. 300 manuscripts written before AD 1000 in Ireland, in Irish script, or with Irish connections (often by Irish 'peregrini' on the Continent). Described with STANDARD Wikidata properties - P31 instance-of, P195 collection, P217 shelfmark, P571 inception (xsd:gYear), P1071 location-of-creation, P2048/P2049 height/width, P1574 exemplar-of - over wd:Q* values, every one of which carries an English rdfs:label fetched from Wikidata (so P1071 reads 'location of creation', Q142 reads 'France'). The named scholars (Eriugena, Sedulius Scottus, Isidore...) carry owl:sameAs to Wikidata, so the graph FEDERATES with the Wikidata datasets. 189 of the manuscripts are digitised: their IIIF manifests (wdt:P6108, from the British Library, Trinity College Dublin, e-codices, IRHT...) render as an in-table image viewer - click a folio for the lightbox. Plus mira: name / script / folios / contents (full-text indexed). Each manuscript is also tagged with MIrA's INCLUSION CRITERIA (mira:category, straight from the project's /about page) - Script: Irish (148), Origin: Ireland (106), Vernacular Old-Irish content (168 glossed pages across 84 manuscripts), Named Irish scribe (41), Exemplar: Irish, Text of Irish origin, plus the 'Insular (Irish?)' outline categories - so you can query exactly why each book is in the corpus. The catalogue draws on the standard palaeographical reference works (Bernhard Bischoff's Katalog der festländischen Handschriften and Südostdeutschen Schreibschulen, E. A. Lowe's Codices Latini Antiquiores); the RDF data was developed by Sudhansu Bala Das, funded by a Research Ireland Laureate award and the Insight Research Ireland Centre for Data Analytics. ~5k triples, embedded (instant, offline). Built from the padraicmoran/MIrA RDF dump + per-manuscript XML by scripts/mira_to_nt.py. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 - non-commercial; cite as Pádraic Moran, Manuscripts with Irish Associations (MIrA), v1.0 (2026), https://mira.ie.

examples.title: Manuscripts you can SEE (IIIF)
examples.tip: 189 of MIrA's manuscripts are digitised. The ?iiif column holds each one's IIIF manifest (wdt:P6108) from its holding library - the British Library, Trinity College Dublin, e-codices, the IRHT... The playground renders it as an in-table image viewer: page the folios with the ‹ › arrows, and CLICK a folio for the lightbox (enlarged page, prev/next, the manifest link and its metadata). ?manuscript is the shelfmark.

examples.title: Where early Irish books were made
examples.tip: wdt:P1071 'location of creation', resolved to its Wikidata label. Ireland leads (100), then Bobbio - the monastery Columbanus founded in Italy, a hub of Irish learning abroad - then France, Italy, Germany and Salzburg: the trail of the Irish 'peregrini' who carried their book-culture across early-medieval Europe.

examples.title: The scholars, linked to Wikidata
examples.tip: MIrA reconciles its named people to Wikidata with owl:sameAs - John Scottus Eriugena, Sedulius Scottus, Isidore, Dúngal... ?wikidata is a clickable link. Because of this alignment the dataset FEDERATES: add a Wikidata source with '+ Add source' and the ids join across both graphs.

examples.title: Cross-source JOIN: MIrA people × live Wikidata
examples.tip: The real thing: ONE query split across TWO sources and JOINED. MIrA answers the first two patterns (owl:sameAs + the person's name); LIVE Wikidata answers ?wd wdt:P106 ?occ (their occupations); they meet on the shared ?wd. The playground routes each pattern to the source that can answer it - by predicate AND variable provenance, so the SECOND rdfs:label correctly goes to Wikidata (where ?occ lives), not MIrA - then bound-joins. This is NOT union (run-everywhere-and-merge); it's a genuine cross-source join. Wikidata is pre-added as a live SPARQL endpoint (see the Sources strip). Result: Eriugena -> theologian/translator, Isidore -> polymath/musicologist, Sedulius Scottus -> poet/grammarian.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX owl: <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX wdt: <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/>
SELECT ?person ?occupation WHERE {
  ?p owl:sameAs ?wd ; rdfs:label ?person .
  ?wd wdt:P106 ?occ . ?occ rdfs:label ?occupation .
  FILTER(LANG(?occupation) = "en")
} LIMIT 40

examples.title: ★ SPARQL SERVICE: scholars' lifespans from live Wikidata
examples.tip: The W3C way to federate, now supported by the ENGINE itself: SERVICE <endpoint> { … } inside the query ships that block to live Wikidata and joins the answers back on the shared ?wd. MIrA's owl:sameAs supplies the Wikidata ids; the VALUES pins three early-medieval scholars — Isidore of Seville (Q166876), John Scottus Eriugena (Q184500) and Sedulius Scottus (Q2609522) — because the block is sent AS WRITTEN, so keep it selective (don't ask Wikidata for every birth date it knows). OPTIONAL inside the block works too: the dates of death come back where Wikidata has them. Compare with the 'Cross-source JOIN' example above — same goal, but there the PLAYGROUND splits one pattern set across sources; here the split is written into the query, per the spec.

examples.title: Same join, but via a shareable mapping linkset
examples.tip: The SAME person -> occupation join, but the LINKS now live in their OWN file: the mira-wikidata SSSOM linkset (skos:exactMatch + provenance), federated in. THREE sources - the linkset answers ?p skos:exactMatch ?wd, MIrA the name, live Wikidata the occupation - routed by predicate AND variable provenance, then bound-joined. This is how mappings are SHARED in the community (SSSOM): a small, citable, queryable artifact decoupled from both datasets, rather than baked into one. Hit 🔍 Plan to see the 3-way routing before it runs.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX wdt: <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/>
SELECT ?person ?occupation WHERE {
  ?p skos:exactMatch ?wd .
  ?p rdfs:label ?person .
  ?wd wdt:P106 ?occ . ?occ rdfs:label ?occupation .
  FILTER(LANG(?occupation) = "en")
} LIMIT 40

datasets.label: bioexplora.rete - 207k natural-history specimens (Museu de Ciencies Naturals de Barcelona, Darwin Core, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The OPEN natural-history collections of the Museu de Ciencies Naturals de Barcelona (bioexplora.cat) as one queryable graph - 207,163 SPECIMENS in Darwin Core across the museum's six collections: arthropods (MCNB-Art, 82,900), molluscs (MCNB-Malac, 50,083), paleontology (MGB, 32,581), vertebrates (MCNB-Cord, 31,954), the tissue bank and general zoology. Every specimen carries its full taxonomy (kingdom -> species), catalogue number, collector, date, locality, georeference and type status, expressed with the REAL Darwin Core term IRIs (dwc:scientificName, dwc:family, dwc:decimalLatitude...) - i.e. the museum's own properties. 13,543 specimens are PHOTOGRAPHED: the IIIF images (museum server, CORS-open) render inline; 43,826 are GEOREFERENCED as GeoSPARQL points (switch Output -> Map); 672 are name-bearing TYPE specimens. Plus two media layers: 667 skull and bone 3D SCANS (the Atles osteologic) linking out to their Sketchfab viewers, and 173 nature SOUND recordings that play inline (CC BY-NC-ND, by Eloisa Matheu via Xeno-canto - NOT the MCNB). 7.19M triples, remote-lazy over HTTP range from the bucket. Harvested KEYLESS from GBIF (the museum publishes Darwin Core archives on ipt.gbif.es), the Sketchfab account laboratorinatura, and Xeno-canto, by scripts/bioexplora_to_nt.py. CC BY 4.0 - credit the Museu de Ciencies Naturals de Barcelona (the audio layer excepted).

examples.title: The collection at a glance
examples.tip: The museum's six collections by specimen count: arthropods (MCNB-Art, 82,900) and molluscs (MCNB-Malac, 50,083) dominate, then paleontology (MGB), vertebrates (MCNB-Cord), the tissue bank and general zoology. 207,163 Darwin Core specimens in all.

examples.tip: ~9,000 specimens are photographed. The ?photo column renders INLINE — molluscs, crustaceans, insects, fossils. Photos are mirrored to the bucket as fast WebP (p:preview, ~10-40 KB; the museum's source link is p:image), and ?collector comes from the shared Agent node. CC BY 4.0, credit the Museu de Ciencies Naturals de Barcelona.

examples.title: See it, hear it, place it — photo + sound + map
examples.tip: One row, four media, joined THROUGH THE GRAPH: a photographed+georeferenced specimen and a Xeno-canto recording that hang off the SAME species Taxon node (?spec p:taxon ?t, ?rec p:taxon ?t) — no string matching. A bird like the Great Crested Grebe shows its specimen photo (WebP), its call (inline player) and where it was collected (click the map cell for a full zoomable map). Stay in Table view to see all four.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX p: <https://bioexplora.cat/prop/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX geo: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>
SELECT ?species ?photo ?sound ?location WHERE {
  ?t p:rank "species" ; rdfs:label ?species .
  ?spec p:taxon ?t ; p:preview ?photo ; geo:asWKT ?location .
  ?rec p:taxon ?t ; p:audio ?sound .
} LIMIT 24

examples.title: The taxonomic tree (family › genus › species)
examples.tip: The taxonomy is now a real GRAPH, not flat strings: every name is a Taxon node linked to its parent rank via p:parentTaxon. This walks species → its genus → its family, one row per species placed in the tree.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX p: <https://bioexplora.cat/prop/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?family ?genus ?species WHERE {
  ?sp p:rank "species" ; rdfs:label ?species ; p:parentTaxon ?g .
  ?g rdfs:label ?genus ; p:parentTaxon ?f .
  ?f p:rank "family" ; rdfs:label ?family .
} ORDER BY ?family ?genus LIMIT 40

examples.title: Walk a whole family down to its species
examples.tip: A TRANSITIVE traversal: p:parentTaxon+ collects every species under a family in one hop, however many ranks deep. Change 'Cerambycidae' (longhorn beetles) to Carabidae, Helicidae (snails), Muridae (rodents)… to walk any branch.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX p: <https://bioexplora.cat/prop/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?genus ?species WHERE {
  ?fam p:rank "family" ; rdfs:label "Cerambycidae" .
  ?sp p:parentTaxon+ ?fam ; p:rank "species" ; rdfs:label ?species ; p:parentTaxon ?g .
  ?g rdfs:label ?genus .
} ORDER BY ?genus LIMIT 40

examples.tip: Collectors are shared Agent nodes (dwc:recordedBy) you can count and traverse. José Fernández de Villalta leads with ~32,000 records, ahead of the malacologists Rius Dalmau and Gasull. 3,876 named collectors in all.

examples.tip: 43,826 specimens are georeferenced (GeoSPARQL points). Switch Output -> Map to see where the holdings were collected across the world — Catalonia and Spain dominate, with material from Morocco, Mexico, France and beyond. Shows up to 3,000 points.

examples.title: ★ FEDERATED: specimen → its country's boundary polygon
examples.tip: A CROSS-SOURCE join, the whole point of federation: bioexplora has the specimens (dwc:countryCode), geoadmin (auto-added as a source) has the country polygons. The query routes each block of patterns to its own dataset and joins on the ISO code — so every specimen pulls in the boundary polygon of the country it was collected in. Output → Map plots them as areas; Table view shows each boundary as a clickable mini-map. This is how you 'get the geospatial column' from another graph.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX dwc: <http://rs.tdwg.org/dwc/terms/>
PREFIX g: <https://w3id.org/rete/geoadmin/prop/>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX geo: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>
SELECT ?species ?country ?boundary WHERE {
  ?s dwc:scientificName ?species ; dwc:countryCode ?code .
  ?a g:iso ?code ; schema:name ?country ; geo:asWKT ?boundary .
} LIMIT 20

examples.title: Type specimens (the holotypes)
examples.tip: 672 name-bearing TYPE specimens — the single most scientifically important objects in any natural-history collection, because each one anchors a species name. ?type is the kind (Holotype, Paratype, Syntype...), ?cat the catalogue number.

CC BY.

examples.tip: 173 nature sound recordings that PLAY inline (?audio is a player) — owls, warblers, frogs and more across 100 species, each with its full Xeno-canto metadata (common name, genus, country, recordist, behaviour, sex/life stage…) and wired into the same Taxon / Collector / Place graph as the specimens. datasets.label: geoadmin.rete - world admin boundaries (geoBoundaries/OSM, 52k polygons, GeoSPARQL, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: World administrative boundaries with GeoSPARQL geometries, built for FEDERATED geospatial joins — 52k OSM-derived polygons (simplified to ~1 km), a lean 15 MB range-queried lazily. 213 COUNTRIES (ADM0), 3,133 REGIONS/states (ADM1) and 48,362 DISTRICTS (ADM2) as POLYGONS from geoBoundaries (OSM-derived, CC-BY), plus 1,251 populated PLACES as POINTS (Natural Earth) — three admin levels, points and polygons. Each entity carries a name, an ISO 3166-1 code (p:iso/p:country, alpha-2 mapped from geoBoundaries' alpha-3), an admin level (p:adminLevel) and its geometry (geo:asWKT). Add it as a federation source to ANY dataset and JOIN on the country code to pull in the boundary polygon — e.g. attach to every bioexplora specimen the polygon of the country it was collected in, then switch Output → Map. geoBoundaries CC-BY 4.0 (geoboundaries.org); places CC0 (Natural Earth). Built by scripts/geoboundaries_to_nt.py.

examples.title: Countries of the world
examples.tip: All 213 country polygons (geoBoundaries ADM0, OSM-derived). Output → Map draws the world; in Table view each ?boundary cell is a mini-map (coarse ~1 km). Click one to open the full map — it fetches THAT country's fine-detail (~110 m) boundary on demand (multi-LOD: only the polygon you inspect is downloaded in detail).
examples.sparql:
PREFIX g: <https://w3id.org/rete/geoadmin/prop/>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX geo: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>
PREFIX class: <https://w3id.org/rete/geoadmin/class/>
SELECT ?c ?country ?boundary WHERE {
  ?c a class:Country ; schema:name ?country ; geo:asWKT ?boundary .
} LIMIT 200

examples.title: ★ SPARQL SERVICE: capitals from live Wikidata
examples.tip: SPARQL 1.1 federated query, ENGINE-level: the SERVICE block is shipped verbatim to query.wikidata.org and its solutions JOIN the local rows on the shared ?code — geoadmin's ISO 3166-1 code (g:iso, e.g. "ES" for Spain) meets Wikidata's P297 value. No VALUES pinning needed: the block is naturally bounded (~250 countries carry an ISO code). The local file answers the country names; live Wikidata the capitals (P36 + English label): Spain → Madrid, Kenya → Nairobi… Unlike '+ Add source' federation (the playground splitting one pattern set across sources), SERVICE is written INTO the query, per the W3C spec — both now work.

examples.title: ★ Vector tiles (PMTiles next to rete)
examples.tip: Output → Tiles renders a 113 MB PMTiles vector basemap (tippecanoe, true per-zoom LOD) of EVERY admin area — pan/zoom and ADM1→ADM2 detail streams in, only the visible tiles fetched. The features your SPARQL returns light up in green ON the basemap: here Spain's autonomous communities. The tiles draw the geometry; rete answers the query right next to them (option B of the geo-LOD work).

PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX geo: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>
PREFIX class: <https://w3id.org/rete/geoadmin/class/>
SELECT ?s ?region ?boundary WHERE {
  ?s a class:Region ; g:country "ES" ; schema:name ?region ; geo:asWKT ?boundary .
}

datasets.label: geoadmin-tiles.rete - the admin-boundaries graph AND a PMTiles vector basemap in ONE file
datasets.description: The SAME world-admin graph as geoadmin, but with a PMTiles vector-tile archive EMBEDDED as a section inside the one .rete file (geo-LOD 'option C'). One immutable, content-hashed, HTTP-range-queryable file holds BOTH: run SPARQL on the RDF graph, then switch Output → Tiles and the map range-reads its vector tiles from a kind-7 section of the very same file (no separate .pmtiles, no second request target). The .rete reader ignores the unknown section, so the graph opens exactly as before; the browser parses the 1 KB header to find the tile section's byte offset and faults tiles from there. GeoSPARQL has no native tiling — this is the experiment of carrying pre-tiled vector geometry next to the graph in one range-served file. Tiles built with tippecanoe (z0-9, true per-zoom LOD) and embedded by scripts/embed_tiles.py.

examples.title: ★ Graph + vector tiles in ONE .rete (option C)
examples.tip: This dataset is ONE .rete file that holds BOTH the RDF graph AND a PMTiles vector basemap (a kind-7 section). The SPARQL below runs on the graph; Output → Tiles range-reads the vector tiles from the SAME file (the browser parses the 1 KB header for the section's byte offset, then faults tiles from there). The features the query returns light up in green — here Spain's regions. One immutable, content-hashed, range-queryable file = graph + map tiles.

datasets.label: smithsonian3d.rete - 2,199 interactive 3D models (Smithsonian Open Access, CC0, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: 2,199 interactive 3D MODELS from the Smithsonian Open Access program (CC0, public domain) - every object streams a Draco-compressed .glb you can rotate, zoom and inspect right in the results table (the 🧊 3D viewer). The collection spans the Institution: the National Museum of Natural History dominates (primate and animal CRANIA, mandibles, fossils and zoological specimens - Hylobates, Pongo, fossil whales), alongside famous objects from the National Air and Space Museum (the Apollo Command Module Columbia, modelled inside and out), American History, the National Portrait Gallery (Abraham Lincoln's life masks), Cooper Hewitt, African American History and the Freer|Sackler. Each model carries its title, the holding museum unit, its catalogue number, and a link (?record) to the full Smithsonian record. Built KEYLESS from the public smithsonian-open-access S3 bucket (the 3d/ prefix - each model a Voyager scene.svx.json listing Low/Medium/High Draco .glb derivatives) by scripts/smithsonian3d_to_nt.py, taking the Medium-quality mesh for streaming; the .glb files are served with CORS from Amazon S3 so they render inline. 15k triples, remote-lazy from the bucket, with lossless Parquet / DuckDB / SQLite table companions beside it for the Explore tab (the Model3D table holds every object). CC0 1.0 - free to use, share and remix; credit the Smithsonian.

datasets.label: lineara.rete - the Linear A corpus (undeciphered Minoan script, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The complete surviving corpus of LINEAR A - the still-undeciphered script of Bronze-Age Minoan Crete (c. 1800-1450 BC), used for palace administration and religious dedications. 1,721 inscriptions (clay tablets, roundels, sealings, libation vessels) from Haghia Triada, Khania, Phaistos, Knossos, Zakros and beyond, each linked to its findspot, scribe, support type and Minoan period, with the Linear A Unicode transcription and the Latin transliteration. The analytical heart is the SIGN and WORD layer: every document is connected to the 375 distinct signs and 1,314 word-sequences it carries (6,039 sign-attestations, 4,100 word-attestations), so you can study sign frequencies, recurring sequences and sign co-occurrence - the main tools for probing an undeciphered script. KU-RO ('total') and KI-RO ('deficit'), the two Linear A words scholars do agree on, are right there at the bottom of the accounts. 67 of the artifacts also LINK (prop:model3d) to the ERC INSCRIBE project's high-resolution interactive 3D scans (3DHOP viewers, University of Bologna) - HT 29, the Khania (KH) and Phaistos (PH) tablets, plus nodules, roundels and a vessel - so you can rotate and measure the actual clay. A second archive, the PAITO Project (Sapienza, Prof. A. Greco; prop:paito), is linked for the Haghia Triada sealings (per-artifact) and the Phaistos corpus (catalogue). Text after the transcriptions of Louis Godart & Jean-Pierre Olivier (GORILA, Ecole Francaise d'Athenes) and the tabulation of George Douros; compiled by mwenge as the LinearA Explorer (github.com/mwenge/lineara.xyz). 38k triples, embedded (instant, offline). Built by scripts/lineara_to_nt.js + scripts/lineara_inscribe.js. Scholarly/educational derivative with full attribution - inscription IMAGES are (c) Ecole Francaise d'Athenes and the 3D MODELS are (c) INSCRIBE / Universita di Bologna (all rights reserved, non-profit scientific use); NEITHER is included here, only references/links; the source repo states no explicit license, so attribute GORILA / Douros / mwenge / INSCRIBE and treat as non-commercial research data.

examples.title: The shape of the corpus
examples.tip: The seven kinds of thing in the graph: 1,721 Inscriptions, 1,314 distinct word-sequences, 375 Signs, 102 Scribes, 52 Sites, plus Support and Period. Because Linear A is undeciphered, 'Word' and 'Sign' mean recurring graphic sequences, not known vocabulary.

examples.title: The most common signs
examples.tip: How often each sign is attested across the whole corpus. KA, KU, SI and A lead — the workhorse syllabograms of the Minoan script. Entries like *301 are Douros/GORILA catalogue numbers for signs that have no agreed phonetic value (the script is undeciphered).

examples.title: Where the tablets were found
examples.tip: Findspots, by document count. Haghia Triada — the great Minoan villa archive in south Crete — dominates with 1,110 inscriptions, followed by the Khania, Phaistos, Knossos and Zakros palaces. Most surviving Linear A is administrative clay from a handful of Cretan centres.

examples.title: Cross-referenced to the 3D & photo archives
examples.tip: The corpus links out to two scholarly digital archives. prop:model3d → the ERC INSCRIBE project's interactive 3D scans (67 artifacts, University of Bologna; rotate and measure the actual clay — e.g. HT 29). prop:paito → the PAITO Project (Sapienza, Prof. Alessandro Greco): per-artifact pages for the Haghia Triada sealings (HT Wa …) and the Phaistos catalogue (tablets / clay sealings / vases — individual pages forthcoming). Both columns are clickable; HT Wa 1561 has both. The scans/photos are © their projects — acknowledge them; the graph stores links, not media.

examples.title: The sequences that recur across the corpus
examples.tip: The word-sequences attested in the most documents — the recurring administrative vocabulary of Minoan accounting. KU heads it, and the famous KU-RO ('total', see the next example) and KI-RO ('deficit') are in the list. Fraction signs (¹⁄₂ …) appear because the accounts record measured quantities.

examples.title: KU-RO — the Minoan word for 'total'
examples.tip: Full-text search (a text index backs it) over the Latin transliteration. KU-RO is the one Linear A word almost everyone agrees on: it means 'total', and it closes an account the way a sum line does — here 34 tablets end with it. Its companion KI-RO means 'deficit / owed'. Change 'KU-RO' to 'KI-RO' or 'SA-RA₂' to follow a different term.

examples.title: Signs that travel with KU
examples.tip: Sign co-occurrence: which signs share a document with KU, and in how many. Since Linear A cannot be read, this distributional method — which signs cluster together — is one of the main tools for probing the script's structure. PA, RO, DA, NA and TA are KU's commonest companions.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX la: <https://lineara.xyz/prop/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?sign (COUNT(DISTINCT ?i) AS ?sharedDocs) WHERE {
  ?i la:sign ?ku . ?ku rdfs:label "KU" .
  ?i la:sign ?o . ?o rdfs:label ?sign .
  FILTER(?o != ?ku)
} GROUP BY ?sign ORDER BY DESC(?sharedDocs) LIMIT 20

examples.title: Documents sharing the term SA-RA₂
examples.tip: Switch Output → Graph. A star of the 20 documents that share the sequence SA-RA₂ — one of the most-discussed Linear A terms (a transaction heading or commodity, found across several sites). Linking documents by a shared sequence is how scholars hunt for genres, scribal habits and the hand of single administrators.

datasets.label: nomisma.rete - coinage of Alexander the Great (PELLA)
datasets.description: PELLA - Coinage of Alexander the Great and the Macedonian kingdom, from Nomisma.org. 7,228 ancient Greek coin TYPES struck under Philip II, Alexander III, Philip III Arrhidaeus and the Diadochi (Cassander, Lysimachus, Ptolemy I), spanning 359-65 BC. Each type links by real IRIs to its mint (~150 cities from Pella and Amphipolis to Babylon, Sardis, Sidon and Susa), issuing authority, material (silver/gold/bronze), denomination (tetradrachm, drachm, stater...), region, and start/end dates as xsd:gYear. Every mint/authority/material/denomination/region carries an English rdfs:label, so the graph is fully self-describing. ~53,535 triples, embeds to ~150 KB. ODbL 1.0 (PELLA coin data) + CC-BY 3.0 (Nomisma vocabulary); attribute the American Numismatic Society / Nomisma.org.

datasets.label: mimotext.rete - French Enlightenment novels + stylometry
datasets.description: MiMoTextBase, a Wikibase of French Enlightenment novels (c. 1751-1800) from the Trier Center for Digital Humanities. A self-contained literary graph: 1,774 works linked to authors (956 people), publication dates and places, genres, languages, narrative form and location, and 375 thematic concepts (4,096 work->theme edges). Its distinctive layer is computational: 520 work-to-work STYLOMETRIC SIMILARITY edges (a Burrows-Delta neighbourhood of which novels read alike), plus 191 scholarship-mention edges. English labels for every entity. ~25,155 triples, ~828 KB Turtle -> embeds. A browsable network of who wrote what, which novels are thematically and stylistically close, and which scholarship discusses them together. CC0 (public domain).

examples.title: What is in this graph?
examples.tip: Counts the main entity kinds (literary works, people, themes, spatial concepts) so you see the shape of the literary network at a glance.

examples.title: Most common themes across the novels
examples.tip: Ranks thematic concepts (P36 'about') by how many distinct novels treat them - the dominant motifs of the Enlightenment novel (sentiment, sentimentalism, travel, love).

examples.title: Baculard d'Arnaud's novels, by year, with genre
examples.tip: Lists the works of the most prolific author in this subset - Baculard d'Arnaud (41 novels) - with publication year (from xsd:dateTime P9) and genre. Author names are stored 'SURNAME, Given', so the match uses CONTAINS on the family name.

examples.title: Novels that share the most themes
examples.tip: Finds the pair of novels with the largest overlap of shared thematic concepts - a thematic 'bridge' between two books.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX wdt: <http://data.mimotext.uni-trier.de/prop/direct/>
PREFIX rdfs:<http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?novelA ?novelB (COUNT(?t) AS ?sharedThemes) WHERE {
  ?a wdt:P36 ?t . ?b wdt:P36 ?t . FILTER(STR(?a) < STR(?b))
  ?a rdfs:label ?novelA FILTER(LANG(?novelA)="en")
  ?b rdfs:label ?novelB FILTER(LANG(?novelB)="en")
} GROUP BY ?novelA ?novelB ORDER BY DESC(?sharedThemes) LIMIT 10

examples.title: Stylometrically closest novels
examples.tip: The 520 computed P49 stylometric-similarity edges link novels close in writing style (a Burrows-Delta neighbourhood). This lists labelled novel - neighbour pairs. In this subset the similarity is a direct work-to-work edge; the distance value itself is not carried.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX wdt: <http://data.mimotext.uni-trier.de/prop/direct/>
PREFIX rdfs:<http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?novel ?stylisticNeighbour WHERE {
  ?a wdt:P49 ?b .
  ?a rdfs:label ?novel FILTER(LANG(?novel)="en")
  ?b rdfs:label ?stylisticNeighbour FILTER(LANG(?stylisticNeighbour)="en")
} LIMIT 20

examples.title: Author ego-network: Baculard d'Arnaud -> novels -> genre
examples.tip: Builds a small subgraph of one author (Baculard d'Arnaud), their novels, and each novel's genre - rendered as a node-link diagram.
