shacl_shapes.tip: MiMoText's distinctive layer is 520 stylometric-similarity edges. Every novel in that style network should carry a label and name its author. SHACL flags 48 nodes that don't.

shacl_shapes.title: Novels with an author carry a date
shacl_shapes.tip: Every work that names an author should also carry a publication date — a few are undated.

shacl_shapes.title: Themed works are labelled
shacl_shapes.tip: Every work that has a theme should carry a label.

shacl_shapes.title: Works with a genre are labelled
shacl_shapes.tip: Every work that records a genre should carry a label.

datasets.label: mmm.rete - the full Mapping Manuscript Migrations provenance graph (23.3M triples, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The ENTIRE Mapping Manuscript Migrations (MMM) graph as one range-queried .rete: 23,349,356 triples over CIDOC-CRM / FRBRoo, unifying the Schoenberg Database (SDBM), Bibale (IRHT) and Medieval Manuscripts in Oxford (Bodleian) into one provenance graph of medieval and Renaissance manuscripts. Each manuscript is an frbroo:F4_Manifestation_Singleton with its production event (E12, with time-span and place), former/current owners (crm:P51 -> E21 persons and E40 organisations), the works/expressions it carries (mmm:manuscript_work), physical detail (material, folios, lines), a shelfmark (mmm:catalog_or_lot_number) and the catalogue/source records that document it (crm:P70i). Places are TGN entities carrying WGS84 coordinates. The MMM metadata ontology is merged in (class/property labels for the Schema view) and a type pyramid + Dataset Card are embedded. Queried lazily over HTTP range - the browser fetches only the dictionary chunks and index tiles each query touches, never the 141 MB whole. Featured here: Cambridge, University Library, MS Gg.1.1 (SDBM entry 212926), the 14th-century trilingual compendium ('A large collection of poetry', parchment, 633 folios). CC BY-NC 4.0 - non-commercial, attribute MMM (seco.cs.aalto.fi). Pick SELECTIVE shapes (a bound manuscript, a bound owner/collection, a shelfmark) for snappy lazy reads; whole-predicate aggregates over 23M triples scan far more.

examples.title: MS Gg.1.1 - the trilingual compendium's full record
examples.tip: Every fact MMM holds about Cambridge, University Library, MS Gg.1.1 - the 14th-century trilingual compendium of texts (SDBM entry 212926). A bound subject is the most selective shape: SPO routing fetches only this manuscript's tiles, a few HTTP ranges of the 141 MB file. You'll see the work it carries, its owners, shelfmark, material (parchment), folio/line counts and the Cambridge catalogue that documents it.

examples.title: MS Gg.1.1 - the trilingual texts inside (Latin, French, English)
examples.tip: What the 'trilingual compendium' actually carries: the work 'A large collection of poetry' and the THREE languages SDBM records for its expression via crm:P72_has_language - Latin, French and English. That mix (Latin + Anglo-Norman French + Middle English) is exactly what makes Cambridge UL MS Gg.1.1 famous. All bound to one manuscript, so it stays a selective lazy read.

examples.title: MS Gg.1.1 - its journey across the world
examples.tip: The manuscript's migration - the very thing MMM maps. Made in 14th-century England (production 1300-1401), MS Gg.1.1's recorded owners span 'Cambridge, University' (England) and 'Washington' (United States), and its last-known location is back at Cambridge with WGS84 coordinates: a medieval book that crossed the Atlantic and seven centuries. UNION gathers the ownership stops and the final location into one result.

examples.title: MS Gg.1.1 - work, owners and shelfmark
examples.tip: The compendium's text ('A large collection of poetry', SDBM's terse title), its shelfmark 'Gg. 1. 1.' and its two recorded owners (Cambridge, University; Washington), resolved through skos:prefLabel. One row per owner. Everything is bound to one manuscript, so it stays a selective lazy read.

examples.title: MS Gg.1.1 - provenance ego-network
examples.tip: Switch Output -> Graph. A small star around MS Gg.1.1: the work it carries, its owners, its material (parchment) and its shelfmark. Each OPTIONAL lets an edge appear only if present, drawing one manuscript's provenance as a node-link card.

examples.title: Other trilingual manuscripts (Latin + French + English), and where they are now
examples.tip: Gg.1.1's exact language profile, generalised across the corpus: manuscripts whose text is recorded in ALL THREE of Latin, French and English. SDBM's language IRIs are shared, so this is a three-way intersection on crm:P72_has_language - 160 manuscripts qualify - paired with their last-known location (often London or Oxford). A real multi-join: carries -> expression -> three languages, then where each ended up.

examples.title: The rare company MS Gg.1.1 keeps - the 3 manuscripts owned by 'Washington'
examples.tip: Gg.1.1 has two recorded owners: the University of Cambridge (1,190 manuscripts) and an obscure 'Washington' (only 3). Follow the rarer one backwards (reverse crm:P51) to surface the unlikely trio it sits among - a book of English statutes (Statuta Angliae, Edward III & Richard II), a Bible, and Gg.1.1's own 'large collection of poetry'. A bound owner keeps this a selective lazy read.

examples.title: MS Gg.1.1's owner, the University of Cambridge, across the linked-data web
examples.tip: Follow Gg.1.1's owner outward. The University of Cambridge is reconciled (owl:sameAs) to SIX authority files - Wikidata (Q35794), VIAF, the BnF, the US Library of Congress, the German GND and the French IdRef. Each ?authority is a real web IRI, so the table links straight out to it. This is how MMM threads its actors into the wider linked-data web.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX crm: <http://erlangen-crm.org/current/>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
PREFIX owl: <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#>
SELECT ?owner ?authority WHERE {
  <http://ldf.fi/mmm/manifestation_singleton/sdbm_orphan_212926> crm:P51_has_former_or_current_owner ?o .
  ?o skos:prefLabel ?owner ; owl:sameAs ?authority .
}

examples.title: How typical are Gg.1.1's three languages? (Latin vs French vs English)
examples.tip: Begin at Gg.1.1's own three languages, then fan out across the WHOLE graph to count how many manuscripts carry each: Latin ~121,600 (the universal language of medieval learning), French ~12,500, and English just ~5,900 - the vernaculars, English the rarest of the three. The heaviest query here: it walks every manuscript in those languages, so run it to watch the engine work, not for a quick answer.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX crm: <http://erlangen-crm.org/current/>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
SELECT ?language (COUNT(DISTINCT ?ms) AS ?manuscripts) WHERE {
  <http://ldf.fi/mmm/manifestation_singleton/sdbm_orphan_212926> crm:P128_carries ?gg .
  ?gg crm:P72_has_language ?lang . ?lang skos:prefLabel ?language .
  ?other crm:P72_has_language ?lang . ?ms crm:P128_carries ?other .
} GROUP BY ?language ORDER BY DESC(?manuscripts)

examples.title: Cambridge University Library - the Gg manuscripts
examples.tip: Manuscripts documented in 'A Catalogue of the Manuscripts preserved in the University Library, Cambridge' (collection sdbm_33357), with their shelfmarks - the Gg.1.x series that MS Gg.1.1 sits in (Gg.1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.5, 1.6, 1.7 ...). A bound object on crm:P70i_is_documented_in routes to just that catalogue's tiles, so it stays a selective lazy read.

examples.title: Manuscripts produced in England
examples.tip: Bind the place 'England' by name, then walk the CIDOC-CRM production event backwards (P7_took_place_at <- E12_Production -> P108_has_produced) to the manuscripts made there. Many now live elsewhere - several here are in the BnF in Paris - which is exactly the migration MMM traces. England produced ~14,650 of the graph's manuscripts.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX crm: <http://erlangen-crm.org/current/>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
SELECT ?msLabel WHERE {
  ?place skos:prefLabel "England" .
  ?prod crm:P7_took_place_at ?place ; crm:P108_has_produced ?ms .
  ?ms skos:prefLabel ?msLabel .
} LIMIT 100

examples.title: Where were manuscripts produced?
examples.tip: Counts manuscripts by production place through the CIDOC-CRM production event (E12_Production -> P7_took_place_at): Italy ~16k, England ~15k, France ~11k, then cities like Paris, Florence and Venice. An aggregate over the whole production relation scans many tiles - heavier than the bound examples above, but still streamed lazily, never a full download.

examples.title: Predicate totals (the shape of the graph)
examples.tip: Which CIDOC-CRM / FRBRoo predicates carry the provenance across all 23.3M triples - ownership (P51), production (P108/P7), documentation (P70i), the works carried. This scans the whole graph, so it's the heaviest example: switch the strategy to Progressive to read it from the embedded pyramid instead of a full scan.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p (COUNT(*) AS ?triples) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o } GROUP BY ?p ORDER BY DESC(?triples) LIMIT 30

shacl_shapes.title: Manuscripts record their provenance
shacl_shapes.tip: Provenance completeness over CIDOC-CRM: every manuscript (F4_Manifestation_Singleton) should carry a label, a former-or-current owner (a person) and a production date. On the full 23.3M-triple graph this targets every manuscript, so it is heavy - use the lazy remote path (it fetches only the shapes' targets) or run it on a bound subset; real provenance is incomplete, so expect many violations.

shacl_shapes.title: Every person is named
shacl_shapes.tip: Every CIDOC-CRM E21_Person should carry a skos:prefLabel. The actor list conforms.

shacl_shapes.title: Manuscripts name a work
shacl_shapes.tip: Every manuscript (F4_Manifestation_Singleton) should record the work it manifests.

shacl_shapes.title: Places are geolocated
shacl_shapes.tip: Every CIDOC-CRM E53_Place should carry WGS84 lat/long coordinates.

datasets.label: antarctic-expeditions.rete - Heroic-Age expeditions, crews & ships
datasets.description: Heroic-Age Antarctic exploration as an explorable social graph: 6 landmark expeditions (Discovery, Nimrod, Terra Nova, Endurance, Australasian, Belgian, 1897-1917) linked by ex:participant to ~76 crew, by ex:vessel to their 5 ships, and by ex:leader to their commanders (Scott, Shackleton, Mawson, de Gerlache). Each expedition carries ex:startYear/ex:endYear. Because expeditions share personnel and ships, genuine multi-hop paths exist (shared-crew bridges, leaders who served on earlier voyages). IRIs stay as wikidata.org/entity so nodes round-trip to live Wikidata. CC0. Pairs with the atlas 'Heroic-Age Sites' overlay: the huts and deaths on the map are where these crews lived and died.

examples.title: Shape of the expedition graph
examples.tip: Predicate totals: ex:participant dominates (~76 crew edges), then ex:vessel / ex:leader, plus rdfs:label and ex:startYear/ex:endYear. Shows the 6-expedition / 5-ship / ~76-person skeleton at a glance.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p (COUNT(*) AS ?triples) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o } GROUP BY ?p ORDER BY DESC(?triples)

examples.title: The crew of the Endurance
examples.tip: Bound-subject star on Shackleton's Endurance (Q1162294): every ex:participant with their name. Includes Mrs. Chippy, the ship's cat, a genuine P710 participant.

PREFIX wd: <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/>

datasets.label: wikidata-xxl - 600M-triple Wikidata as 6 federated .rete shards (ONE logical graph, sharded)
datasets.description: The SHARDED-RETE model at scale: one logical Wikidata graph too big to build as a single file, split into 6 INDEPENDENT --no-pyramid .rete shards (100M triples / ~906 MB each, ~5.4 GB total) that the playground AUTO-FEDERATES — every query fans across all 6 shards (UNION) and the rows merge, so you query it like one dataset. A genuine cross-section of the Wikidata truthy dump (people, places, works, taxa, properties) streamed partition-by-partition from the piebro/wikidata-extraction Parquet (DuckDB httpfs, no full download) and built shard-by-shard with bounded RAM/disk (stream → rete build --no-pyramid → drop the 10 GB N-Triples → next). Each entity carries multilingual rdfs:label / skos:prefLabel / schema:name + schema:description, rdf:type / wdt:P31, and truthy wdt:* statements (occupation P106, etc.); IRIs stay wikidata.org/{entity,prop/direct}/* so nodes round-trip to live Wikidata. This proves the .rete format + client-side federation scale to a dataset BIGGER THAN ANY SINGLE FILE — the path to full Wikidata (~80 shards, ~80 GB) is just more shards. Datatypes are heuristic (typed dateTime + WKT; numbers plain) since WDQS rate-limits the property-datatype map. The fed bar shows '⛓ 6 shards'. Built by scripts/build_wikidata_xxl.sh. CC0 (Wikidata).

The query FANS ACROSS all 6 (UNION) and the rows merge — watch the banner say 'federated 6 sources'. HEAVY: it queries 6 remote ~900 MB R2 objects, so a fan-out can still take a minute. The architecture, not the speed, is the point: a dataset bigger than any single file, queried as one.

datasets.label: chebi-full.rete - the complete ChEBI chemical ontology (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The ENTIRE ChEBI ontology (Chemical Entities of Biological Interest, EMBL-EBI) as one range-queried .rete: 8.83M triples over ~205k chemical classes, their rdfs:subClassOf classification DAG (380k edges), textual definitions (obo:IAO_0000115), exact/related synonyms, ~900k database cross-references (as reified owl:Axiom annotations), and the structural data chemistry needs - molecular formula, charge, average & monoisotopic mass, InChI, InChIKey and SMILES, all under the ChemROF vocabulary (chemrof: https://w3id.org/chemrof/). Queried lazily over HTTP range: the browser fetches only the dictionary chunks and index tiles each query touches, never the 120 MB whole. CC BY 4.0 (EMBL-EBI). It shares its CHEBI_* class IRIs and rdfs:label / rdfs:subClassOf structure with the chemotion dataset, so the two FEDERATE: pick chebi-full, add chemotion as a second source (the 'Federation' example does this for you), and one SPARQL query resolves terms across both ontologies. Lossless Parquet / DuckDB / SQLite table companions sit beside it in the bucket. Pick selective shapes (a bound molecule, a formula, a subClassOf path) for snappy lazy reads; whole-predicate aggregates scan more.

examples.title: What's in the ontology (predicate totals)
examples.tip: The shape of all of ChEBI in one scan: rdf:type leads (1.2M, mostly the owl:Axiom cross-reference reification), then oboInOwl xrefs/synonyms, rdfs:subClassOf (380k classification edges), rdfs:label (205k), and the ChemROF structural predicates (formula, charge, mass, SMILES, InChI). Summary-answerable - try the Progressive strategy to read it from the pyramid alone.

datasets.label: causenet.rete - a causality graph mined from the web (256M triples, typed + full-text, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: CauseNet-Full (Heindorf et al., CIKM 2020): the complete causality graph mined from Wikipedia and ClueWeb12 - 11,609,890 cause->effect relations over 12,186,310 concepts, with full extraction provenance. Each relation keeps every one of its 24,443,421 source records: the exact sentence the cause/effect pair was found in, the dependency path-pattern it was matched by (e.g. '[[cause]]/N -nsubj caused/VBD +dobj [[effect]]/N'), and the Wikipedia page or ClueWeb12 web page it came from. Concepts are cn:Concept nodes (cn: = https://causenet.org/ontology#) carrying rdfs:label; cn:causes is the direct cause->effect edge (transitive - follow it with Reach for causal chains); each relation is reified as a cn:CausalRelation with cn:support (its true source count) and cn:hasSource links to the source records. 256,133,680 triples (6.39 GB), queried lazily over HTTP range - the browser fetches only the dictionary chunks and index tiles each query touches, never the whole file. CC BY 4.0 (credit Heindorf et al.). Pick SELECTIVE shapes (a bound concept, a bound relation, the evidence for one claim) for snappy lazy reads; whole-graph aggregates scan more. Lossless relations/sources/concepts Parquet/DuckDB/SQLite companions sit beside it in the bucket.

examples.title: What does smoking cause? (effect + evidence)
examples.tip: Everything 'smoking' is claimed to cause, each with cn:support = how many source sentences back the claim, so the best-evidenced effects (cancer, heart disease, death) sort to the top. Two columns: effect + support. Reads the reified cn:CausalRelation, so a bit heavier than the bare-edge version (which was ~57 MB lazy). Swap the IRI for /stress, /obesity, /war.

examples.title: What causes obesity? (cause + evidence)
examples.tip: The reverse direction with evidence: every concept claimed to cause 'obesity', ranked by source count. Columns: cause + support. Swap the effect IRI for /diabetes, /cancer or /depression to mine a different outcome.

examples.title: Best-evidenced causes of cancer
examples.tip: Causes of 'cancer' ranked by how much web evidence backs each claim (cn:support = true source count). Columns: cause + support. Benchmarked lazy cost on the lean file: ~114 MB over HTTP range, ~42 s cold.

examples.title: Causal chain: smoking -> X -> Y
examples.tip: A two-step chain over cn:causes: what smoking causes (column 1), and what each of those in turn causes (column 2) - tracing how one cause cascades. For full transitive closure use the Reach tab on cn:causes; this 2-hop join stays bounded.

examples.title: Effects + evidence sentence (HEAVY, 3 cols)
examples.tip: Three columns - effect, support, and a REAL source sentence CauseNet mined the claim from (cn:hasSource -> cn:sentence). The richest view of a causal claim. HEAVIEST example: 'smoking' has thousands of sources, so it fetches 100s of MB over HTTP range; keep the LIMIT low or pick a narrower cause.

examples.title: Map smoking's effects (graph)
examples.tip: CONSTRUCT a small cause->effect subgraph around 'smoking' for the graph view - the selective bare cn:causes read (~57 MB lazy), rendered as nodes + arrows. Each arrow is a mined causal claim from Wikipedia / ClueWeb12.

shacl_shapes.title: Every causal relation has a cause, an effect and a support count
shacl_shapes.tip: Data-integrity over the reified relations: every cn:CausalRelation must declare exactly one cn:cause and one cn:effect and at least one cn:support. Remote SHACL validates lazily over the shape's targets (range reads) - a broad target class fetches many targets, so give it a moment.

shacl_shapes.title: Every concept is named
shacl_shapes.tip: Every cn:Concept node should carry an rdfs:label (its surface form). Validated lazily over the concept targets via HTTP range.

shacl_shapes.title: Every ClueWeb12 source keeps its sentence and pattern
shacl_shapes.tip: Provenance completeness: every ClueWeb12 source record must keep the sentence it was extracted from and the dependency path-pattern that matched it. Validated lazily over the ClueWeb12 source targets.

datasets.label: jonas.rete - medieval texts & their manuscript witnesses (LostMa-ERC / Jonas)
datasets.description: A knowledge graph of medieval European texts and the manuscripts that transmit them, built from the LostMa-ERC Heurist database derived from Jonas (IRHT-CNRS, the repertory of texts and manuscripts in langue d'oc and d'oil). 234,017 triples over a Heurist record model: 3,738 witnesses (a text attested in a manuscript - with siglum, status, date), 1,128 texts (Lancelot, Tristan, Wolfram's Parzival, the chansons de geste; with language and literary form), 3,153 documents/manuscripts (shelfmark, collection, holding place), 4,253 text parts, 860 physical descriptions, 1,152 places (linked to GeoNames), 575 repositories (linked to VIAF), genres, stories/storyverses, and 71 reconstructed stemmata (openStemmata), over a 4,506-term controlled vocabulary. Every record links back to its live Jonas page via prop:described_at_URL. Queried lazily over HTTP range; the whole file is only ~2 MB, so reads are near-instant. CC0 1.0 (LostMa-ERC; underlying data from Jonas / IRHT-CNRS). Entity IRIs are lostma-erc.github.io/jonas/{id,prop,type,term}/*. This is a curated research subset (the LostMa corpus), not the full ~77k-witness Jonas repertory.

examples.title: What's in the graph (record types)
examples.tip: The shape of the LostMa/Jonas corpus in one scan: 3,738 witnesses, 4,253 text parts, 3,153 manuscripts (documents), 1,152 places, 1,128 texts, plus physical descriptions, repositories, stories, stemmata and a 4,506-term controlled vocabulary. The whole file is ~2 MB, so even this scan is a couple of range reads.

examples.title: Witnesses linking back to their live Jonas page
examples.tip: A URL-ID column: prop:described_at_URL is each witness's permanent link back to the live Jonas repertory (jonas.irht.cnrs.fr/...). It renders as a clickable link - or set the column's type dropdown to Link. Paired with the witness siglum, so every row is a citable handle on the source record.

examples.title: The most-copied medieval texts
examples.tip: Counts the surviving manuscript witnesses per text - the medieval 'bestsellers'. The prose Lancelot leads with 122 witnesses, then Tristan (93), Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival (88) and Willehalm (80), the Roman de Troie, Merlin and the Estoire del Saint Graal. p:is_manifestation_of links each witness to the text it copies.

examples.title: Witnesses of the Lancelot, with their manuscripts
examples.tip: Every manuscript copy of the most-witnessed text, the prose Lancelot: each witness's siglum, the manuscript shelfmark it survives in (p:last_observed_in_doc) and its date. A bound text label keeps it selective - the core philological view, one work seen across all the books that carry it.

examples.title: Texts and the manuscripts that carry them
examples.tip: Walks witness -> text (p:is_manifestation_of) and witness -> manuscript (p:last_observed_in_doc) to show which texts survive in which books, with the witness siglum: the Roman van Limborch, the Roelantslied and the rest, each tied to a shelfmark. The witness IS the join - a text attested in a manuscript.

examples.title: The corpus by language
examples.tip: The LostMa corpus is comparative and multilingual: Old French (fro) 309 texts, Middle High German (gmh) 150, Middle Irish (mga) 92, Middle French (frm) 91, Middle Dutch (dum) 85, Middle English (enm) 81. Each text's language is a controlled-vocabulary term (p:language_term -> skos:prefLabel).

examples.title: Where the manuscripts are held
examples.tip: Follows each manuscript to its holding place (p:location -> the library/place label): the Beinecke, the Leeds Brotherton library and hundreds more. Places carry GeoNames links (owl:sameAs) and repositories carry VIAF, so the books thread out into the linked-data web - switch the place column to Link to follow them.

examples.title: Texts with a reconstructed stemma
examples.tip: The texts whose manuscript tradition has a published stemma codicum (p:in_stemma -> a stemma record with its openStemmata id): Fierabras, Girart de Vienne, Aliscans, Florence de Rome, the Chevalerie Ogier de Danemarche. These genealogies of surviving copies are what LostMa studies to model how texts were lost.

datasets.label: Post Scriptum - Portuguese & Spanish everyday letters, 1500-1800 (CLUL)
datasets.description: Post Scriptum (CLUL, Universidade de Lisboa), via the TEITOK TEI-P5 edition: 3,649 everyday letters in Portuguese & Spanish, 1500-1800 - a historical correspondence network. Each letter (ps:Letter) carries its sender and recipient (ps:sentBy / ps:receivedBy -> 3,265 person nodes), origin & destination places (ps:sentFrom / ps:sentTo), a date (ps:date, reaching back to 1500), language, the modernised body text (full-text indexed for content search), a social/pragmatic classification (ps:letterType: personal / family / friendship / love..., ps:pragmatics: request..., ps:keyword), and foaf:page back to the live TEITOK letter page. Built from the freely-downloadable XML-TEI_P5 bundles (ES/PT x 1500-1800), the TEI source parsed by scripts/postscriptum_to_nt.py. ~63k triples, 5.3 MB, queried lazily over HTTP range. Free (CLUL recognised as author; ELRA licences). Entity IRIs are teitok.clul.ul.pt/postscriptum/{letter,person}/*.

examples.title: Who wrote to whom, and when
examples.tip: The correspondence network: each letter's sender (ps:sentBy) and recipient (ps:receivedBy) resolved to names, with its date - everyday Portuguese & Spanish letters from 1500 onward (Beatriz Carneira -> Francisco de Figueiredo, 1500-06-27). Sort the date column to walk three centuries of private mail.

examples.title: Read a letter online (TEITOK link)
examples.tip: A URL-ID column: foaf:page is each letter's permanent link to its edition on the live TEITOK site - click to read the diplomatic + modernised transcription with manuscript images. Paired with the letter's title (year, sender, recipient). Set the column type to Link if it doesn't auto-detect.

examples.title: Letters by social register
examples.tip: Post Scriptum classifies each letter's relationship (ps:letterType): personal (1,794) dominates, then family (926), friendship (525) and love (270) - the everyday emotional registers of 16th-18th-century correspondence, plus 42 anonymous (denunciations, threats).

examples.title: Search the letters by content
examples.tip: Full-text search over the modernised letter text (a text index backs it). Change the term (here 'amor') to any word to find the letters that use it - the actual language people wrote. Each row is the matching letter's title; add ?text to the SELECT to read the passage.

examples.title: The busiest letter-writers
examples.tip: Rank the 3,265 correspondents by how many surviving letters they sent (ps:sentBy). The network's hubs - writers whose archives preserved many letters (often from Inquisition or judicial cases, which is why the letters survive at all) - rise to the top.

examples.title: What the letters are about (topics)
examples.tip: Post Scriptum tags each letter with keyword terms (ps:keyword) - the recurring themes of everyday early-modern mail. Correspondence itself (448), Family (421), Money (349), Justice (265), Illness (263), Debts (198), Marriage (190): the texture of private life across three centuries. Spanish and Portuguese terms are tagged separately (@es / @pt).

examples.title: Letters by language and century
examples.tip: Each letter's sub-corpus (ps:corpus) encodes language x century: Spanish 1500-1800 (310 / 684 / 938 / 514) and Portuguese 1500-1800 (252 / 430 / 509 / 12). The 17th-18th centuries dominate - when literacy spread and the judicial / Inquisition archives that preserved these letters were most active.

datasets.label: data.bnf.fr - the whole BnF linked open data (716M triples, ONE file)
datasets.description: The COMPLETE data.bnf.fr - the Bibliothèque nationale de France's linked open data (CC0) - as ONE range-queryable .rete (it was 10 federated shards). The official dump's 726,700,333 triples dedup to 673,519,782 unique (matching the BnF's live ~672M store), 194.8M terms, 7.16 GB. Every perimeter in one graph: 4.9M author/person authorities (foaf:Person) with 8.8M owl:sameAs alignments to VIAF / ISNI / IdRef (the authority hub overlapping MMM, Jonas and Biblissima), 2.6M FRBR works, the RAMEAU subject thesaurus, role-typed contributions, places (GeoNames), periodicals, and the 410M-triple modern printed-book catalogue (editions). Carries a types pyramid + planner query_stats, so summary / schema / community queries are answered index-free. Entity IRIs stay as data.bnf.fr/ark:/* so nodes round-trip to the live BnF. Built as a single file with the low-RAM pipeline that made the 726M monolith feasible (it was sharded because the monolith OOM'd a 62 GB host - see dev/low-mem-build.md). Queried lazily over HTTP range: a selective query fetches only the dict chunks and index tiles it touches, never the 7 GB whole; whole-graph aggregates scan more. CC0 1.0 (BnF).

examples.title: Authors and their VIAF / ISNI identity
examples.tip: data.bnf.fr's authority layer: each author (foaf:Person) carries a name and owl:sameAs alignments to VIAF, ISNI and IdRef - the SAME VIAF ids that MMM, Jonas and Biblissima link to, so this is the federation hub for 'who is this author' across every manuscript dataset (8.8M sameAs links). The leading space in some names is BnF's sort form.

examples.title: Authors joined to the works they created
examples.tip: The single-file payoff: a cross-perimeter JOIN the 10 shards could NOT do (federation is union + routing, not term-level joins). Works (dcterms:creator -> an author ARK) join persons (foaf:name) in ONE graph, so 'this author wrote these works' resolves in a single query - no '+ Add source'.

examples.title: RAMEAU subject headings
examples.tip: RAMEAU is the French national subject thesaurus - the controlled vocabulary the BnF indexes everything under. Each heading is a skos:Concept with a prefLabel (and broader/narrower hierarchy in the full graph).

examples.title: What's in the whole BnF (predicate totals)
examples.tip: Predicate totals over the COMPLETE data.bnf.fr - 673.5M unique triples in ONE file (was 10 shards): rdf:type, dcterms:subject (RAMEAU), owl:sameAs (VIAF/ISNI/IdRef), the FRBNF id, titles, contributions, editions. The types pyramid + planner query_stats answer this kind of whole-graph summary index-free.

datasets.label: datos.bne.es - the whole Spanish National Library LOD (267M triples, ONE file)
datasets.description: The COMPLETE datos.bne.es - the Biblioteca Nacional de España's linked open data (CC0) - as ONE range-queryable .rete: 267,052,840 triples (the three official RDF dumps merged - autoridades 47M, bibliográficos 208M, materias 6M), 84M terms, 3.4 GB. The Spanish counterpart of data.bnf.fr. Entities at datos.bne.es/resource/* over the BNE's own ontology (datos.bne.es/def/C* classes, P* properties) plus the RDA registry; subjects are SKOS. The authority layer (persons, corporate bodies, works) carries owl:sameAs alignments to VIAF, ISNI, GND, LoC, IdRef, DBpedia AND data.bnf.fr - so it FEDERATES with the databnf dataset: add databnf as a second source ('+ Add source') and one query joins Spanish to French authorities on their shared VIAF / data.bnf.fr ids. Carries a types pyramid + planner query_stats, so summary / schema / community queries are answered index-free. Built as a single file with the low-RAM pipeline (peak ~25.6 GiB); the dump's ~64k malformed lines (IRIs with a stray '>' or a trailing space) were dropped. Entity IRIs stay datos.bne.es/resource/* so nodes round-trip to the live BNE. Queried lazily over HTTP range. CC0 1.0 (BNE).

examples.title: Authorities and their external identities
examples.tip: The BNE authority layer: each authority carries a name (the BNE ontology's P5001) and owl:sameAs links out to VIAF, ISNI, GND, LoC, IdRef, DBpedia and data.bnf.fr - the same authority hubs the French BnF uses, which is why bne + databnf federate. Here, authorities with a VIAF alignment.

examples.title: What's in the BNE by class
examples.tip: Group every resource by its rdf:type - the BNE's own ontology classes (datos.bne.es/def/C* codes: persons, corporate bodies, works/expressions, and the bibliographic manifestations that are the bulk). The types pyramid answers this whole-graph aggregate index-free.

examples.title: BNE authorities that bridge to data.bnf.fr
examples.tip: The Spanish-to-French bridge: BNE authorities whose owl:sameAs points at a data.bnf.fr id (Alfaro -> data.bnf.fr/10000803, etc.). Switch on the databnf dataset with '+ Add source' and these ids resolve in the French graph too.

examples.title: Federation: authority links across BNE + BnF
examples.tip: Federation is a kind of SPARQL. This pre-loads databnf (the whole data.bnf.fr) as a second source - see the Sources strip. The query asks for owl:sameAs->VIAF links, which BOTH graphs answer, so the result is the UNION of the Spanish (bne) and French (databnf) authority alignments to VIAF - the shared hub identifying the same person across both national libraries. (Cross-source term JOINS are a future feature; this is union + predicate routing.) Remove the databnf chip to query the BNE alone.

examples.title: A profile from the RDA layer (Cervantes)
examples.tip: datos.bne.es describes persons with RDA Elements (www.rdaregistry.info/Elements/a/P501xx): their professions (P50104), birthplace (P50119) and the period they worked in (P50101). Here, everything the RDA layer records for Cervantes - dramatist / novelist / poet / soldier, born in Alcala de Henares, of the Siglo de Oro. Change the name in P5001 to any BNE authority (a bound subject = a selective, fast read).

examples.title: An author's links out (Wikipedia, VIAF, DBpedia)
examples.tip: A URL-ID column: the BNE links each authority to the wider web - rdfs:seeAlso to Wikipedia, owl:sameAs to VIAF, DBpedia, GND, the Library of Congress, IdRef and data.bnf.fr. Here, all of Cervantes's outbound links (they render as clickable cells - set the column type to Link if needed). This is the federation hub: the same ids bne, databnf and Biblissima share to mean the same person.

datasets.label: Biblissima+ - medieval written heritage (full Wikibase, ONE file)
datasets.description: Biblissima+, the French aggregator of medieval & early-modern written heritage, as ONE range-queryable .rete (it was 3 federated shards): 254,203,131 triples over 867,838 Wikibase entities - manuscripts, works, persons, places, printed editions, iconography - harvested from its open per-entity RDF export (Special:EntityData; Biblissima has no bulk dump and its SPARQL is gated). The manuscript / authority hub of this whole constellation; it overlaps the BnF, MMM and Jonas on persons & places. Wikibase model: entities at data.biblissima.fr/entity/Q*, truthy statements via prop/direct/P*, P2 = 'instance of', multilingual rdfs:label / skos:prefLabel. Now a single 667 MB file with a P2-keyed types pyramid (4 semantic-zoom levels) + planner query_stats, so it answers summary / schema / community queries index-free - built with the low-RAM pipeline that made the monolith feasible (it was sharded because the 254M build OOM'd a 62 GB host). Queried lazily over HTTP range. CC-BY 4.0 (Biblissima+, Campus Condorcet).

examples.title: Manuscripts you can SEE (IIIF thumbnails)
examples.tip: The ?iiif column holds a IIIF manifest (prop/direct/P196) - the digitized manuscript at its holding library (Cambridge cudl, e-codices, the Vatican's digi.vatlib.it...). The playground fetches each manifest and renders it as a PAGED viewer right in the table: use the ‹ › buttons or the page box to leaf through the manuscript, and CLICK the image to open a lightbox - an enlarged page with prev/next paging, the manifest link and its metadata (each page faults from the IIIF Image API on demand). ?manuscript is the Biblissima entity, ?label its shelfmark.

examples.title: See manuscripts held in two cities
examples.tip: A richer pull: digitized manuscripts (a IIIF manifest, P196) grouped by their holding collection (P194, whose label is 'City. Library'), filtered to TWO cities - here Paris and Geneve (STRSTARTS on the city prefix). Each ?iiif is a paged viewer (‹ › to leaf through; click to open the lightbox with the enlarged page + manifest metadata). NOTE: Biblissima records the current holding city, not a production->migration path, and these manuscript records carry no production date (P72/P73 'earliest/latest date' sit on other entity types) - for true manuscript MIGRATION between cities over time, see the MMM dataset (which, however, has no images). Swap the two cities for any others (Roma, Oxford, Cambridge...).
examples.sparql:
PREFIX bd: <https://data.biblissima.fr/prop/direct/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?city ?shelfmark ?iiif WHERE {
  ?ms bd:P196 ?iiif ; bd:P194 ?c ; bd:P195 ?shelfmark .
  ?c rdfs:label ?city . FILTER(LANG(?city) = "fr")
  FILTER(STRSTARTS(?city, "Paris") || STRSTARTS(?city, "Gen"))
} ORDER BY ?city LIMIT 24

Whole-graph totals; the P2-keyed types pyramid can answer this kind of summary index-free.

examples.title: Entities by their French label
examples.tip: Biblissima describes manuscripts, works, persons, places and editions - all as Wikibase entities (data.biblissima.fr/entity/Q*) with multilingual labels. Here, every entity carrying a French rdfs:label (persons, saints, instruments, institutions...).

examples.title: Entities grouped by type (instance of)
examples.tip: Group entities by their type (prop/direct/P2 = 'instance of' in the Biblissima Wikibase), resolved to a French label - the composition of the whole graph (manuscripts, works, persons, places, editions...). Full totals now that it is a single file, not a shard.

examples.title: Authority names across languages
examples.tip: Biblissima reconciles persons, works and places into multilingual authorities. Each entity's French rdfs:label paired with a skos:altLabel variant in another script or language (Arabic, Turkish, Italian, English transliterations of the same name) - the cross-lingual name graph that lets a manuscript catalogued in one tradition match a record in another.

datasets.label: Institución Colombina (ARCAS, Sevilla) - Seville cathedral + archdiocese archives, 69,900 ISAD records (remote-lazy)
datasets.description: The archival catalogue (ISAD) of the Institución Colombina, Seville: 69,900 records from the Archivo Catedral de Sevilla (ACS, 27,970) and the Archivo General del Arzobispado de Sevilla (AGAS, 41,930) - the Seville cathedral chapter and diocesan archives, with records reaching back to 1424 (Cathedral liturgical codices) and 1510. 927,788 triples queried lazily over HTTP range. Each record (arcas:ArchivalRecord) carries a title (dcterms:title), one or more dates (dcterms:date), its signatura / call number (arcas:signatura - boxes, 'Caja / NNNN'), the ISAD reference and classification codes (arcas:referenceCode, arcas:classificationCode), its archival level (arcas:level, e.g. 'Unidad documental compuesta'), the archive it belongs to (arcas:inArchive) and its parent in the description hierarchy (dcterms:isPartOf - so the fonds/series/file/item tree reconstructs). A full-text index over the titles powers content search (the marriage-licence series of the Archdiocese, liturgy, capellanías...). Harvested anonymously from the public ARCAS consultation (Baratz 'Albalá 7', a Solr-backed JS portal at albala.icolombina.es) - metadata only; the digital images are not publicly available. Entity IRIs are albala.icolombina.es/arcas/{record,archive}/*. © Institución Colombina (public catalogue metadata).

examples.title: Records per archive
examples.tip: The catalogue holds two archives of the Institución Colombina: the Archivo General del Arzobispado de Sevilla (AGAS, the Seville diocesan archive) with 41,930 records and the Archivo Catedral de Sevilla (ACS, the cathedral chapter) with 27,970. arcas:inArchive links each record to its holding archive, arcas:ArchivalRecord is the record type.

examples.title: The earliest records (15th-16th century)
examples.tip: Filters dates that end in a year 1400-1599 (dates come as '01/01/1424' or just '1424'). The Cathedral's oldest holdings surface: liturgical codices from 1424, chapter acts, and the censos / capellanías / patronatos (rents and chantry endowments) of the early 1500s. Switch the date column sort to read them chronologically.

examples.title: Marriage-licence files of the Archdiocese
examples.tip: Free-text over the record titles (a full-text index backs the search). The Archdiocese's 'expedientes matrimoniales' - marriage-dispensation case files that name the couple and their Andalusian town (e.g. Jerez de la Frontera, Puerto Real) - are the bulk of AGAS and a major genealogical source for western Andalusia.

examples.title: A file and the series it belongs to
examples.tip: dcterms:isPartOf threads every record to its parent in the ISAD description tree, so file -> series -> fonds reconstructs. Here each record paired with the title of the unit that contains it (e.g. a single marriage expediente under 'Expedientes matrimoniales ordinarios de Pueblos. Letra A.').

examples.title: Records by archival level
examples.tip: ISAD describes archives as a hierarchy of levels - fonds, series, file (expediente), item. arcas:level records each unit's level; most of this catalogue is described at the 'unidad documental compuesta' (compound documentary unit) level, with the upper fonds/series levels far fewer.

examples.title: Capellanías & patronatos (chantry endowments)
examples.tip: Text search for 'capellan' over the titles: the capellanías and patronatos - endowed chantries and lay patronages - are a distinctive Cathedral-chapter holding, with their censos, tributos and property deeds. Each row gives the title, its date and the box signatura (arcas:signatura, e.g. 'Caja / 5853 - 2').

datasets.label: Memòria - Spanish Civil War victims & mass graves (open data)
datasets.description: An aggregation of openly-licensed Spanish Civil War 'memoria histórica' datasets into ONE knowledge graph: 99,542 named victims/repressed persons and 2,872 mass graves (fosas), tied together through provinces. 1.21M triples, remote-lazy over HTTP range. Persons (mc:Victim) come from three regional registries - Catalonia's reparació jurídica de víctimes del franquisme (69,834), Catalonia's desapareguts de la Guerra Civil (8,339) and Euskadi's víctimas mortales (21,369) - each carrying name (rdfs:label), sex (mc:sex), age (mc:age), birth & residence municipality/province (mc:bornInMunicipality / mc:bornInProvince / mc:residedIn*), cause/manner of death (mc:cause, e.g. 'Gudari/miliciano muerto en combate', 'Ejecutado por Consejo de Guerra'), sentence (mc:sentence), profession, military unit, and an executed flag (mc:executed). Mass graves (mc:MassGrave) come from the Catalan (1,027, with WGS84 mc:lat/long + GeoSPARQL geometry), Andalusian (615, with historical narratives mc:narrative), Castilla y León (701, with repressor side) and Valencian (529) fosas registries - each with municipality, province (mc:province), victim count (mc:victimCount), status and a link to its official record (foaf:page). 88 provinces (mc:Province) link victims and graves, so you can ask 'which provinces have both the most victims and the most graves'. A full-text index over names powers person search. IRIs are memoria.rete/{persona,fosa,provincia}/*. Aggregated from regional open-data portals (transparenciacatalunya.cat, opendata.euskadi.eus, juntadeandalucia.es, jcyl.es, gva.es) - all CC-BY-style open data; sensitive personal/historical data, attribute the source administrations. NB this is the open regional data, NOT a scrape of any search portal.

examples.title: Victims by province of birth
examples.tip: Counts named victims / repressed persons by province of birth (mc:bornInProvince -> a shared mc:Province node). Barcelona leads with 22,555, then Tarragona, Lleida and Girona - this corpus is Catalonia-heavy (the reparació-jurídica registry), with Múrcia, Almería and València next.

examples.title: How people died (Basque registry)
examples.tip: The Euskadi víctimas registry records a manner of death (mc:cause). Combat deaths lead - 7,322 gudaris/milicianos killed in action and 5,953 on the rebel front - then deaths in captivity, and the executions: extrajudicial killings by rebels (1,143) and by Republicans (957), and 996 shot after court-martial (Consejo de Guerra).

examples.title: Map the mass graves (Catalonia)
examples.tip: Switch Output -> Map (try the new Basemap dropdown to put them on satellite/streets). The 1,027 Catalan fosas carry WGS84 geometry (geo:asWKT) - each point is a documented Civil War mass grave. Stay on Table and the ?w column renders a per-row mini-map (each grave a dot on a small world map). Other regions' graves (Andalucía, Castilla y León, València) are in the graph too but without coordinates in their open data.

examples.title: Largest mass graves by victim count
examples.tip: Graves ordered by mc:victimCount: the largest are in Andalucía - Huelva and Órgiva (Granada) at ~5,000, Málaga ~4,000, Sevilla ~3,600, Granada ~2,992 - reflecting the mass extrajudicial killings of 1936 in the south. Counts are estimates from each regional registry.

examples.title: Find a person by surname
examples.tip: A full-text index over names backs this. Change the literal (here a CONTAINS on 'GARCIA') to any surname to pull matching victims with their birthplace - the personal layer of the registries. Names are stored as 'SURNAME1 SURNAME2, Given'.

examples.title: Provinces with both victims and graves
examples.tip: The province nodes join the two layers. Two sub-aggregates - victims born per province and mass graves per province - joined on the shared mc:Province, so you see where the documented dead and the documented graves coincide. One query instead of two because mc:Province is the join key.

datasets.label: Embassy of the Free Mind - 2,307 hermetic & esoteric books (Bibliotheca Philosophica Hermetica, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The digitized core of the Bibliotheca Philosophica Hermetica - the Ritman Library / Embassy of the Free Mind in Amsterdam, the world's foremost collection on Hermetica, alchemy, Rosicrucianism, Kabbalah, mysticism and Western esotericism (partly funded by Dan Brown). 2,307 rare books (15th-19th c.) harvested KEYLESS from Source Library (sourcelibrary.org, the collection's own reading platform) with full cataloguing: original + English title, author (a linked schema:Person), year (schema:datePublished), publisher / place of publication, language (German 929, Latin 585, English, French, Dutch, Italian, Hebrew...), shelfmark, bibliography references and USTC catalogue links. Every book also carries an AI-written summary + reading-summary and four significance scores (historical / scholarly / visual / accessibility, 0-25 each) plus a 0-100 quality score, a subject index (126,752 dcterms:subject links to SKOS concepts), chapter structure, geocoded publication places (GeoSPARQL points - switch Output to Map) and related-book links. 764,708 page-image URLs render inline from images.sourcelibrary.org (CORS-open), plus one cover thumbnail per book. 5.77M triples, remote-lazy over HTTP range. Modeled with schema.org / Dublin Core / SKOS / GeoSPARQL by scripts/fetch_bph.py + scripts/bph_to_nt.py. CC BY-SA 4.0 - credit the Embassy of the Free Mind / BPH. Full per-page OCR + English translation text (also CC BY-SA 4.0) is gated behind a free Source Library API key and can be added as a second layer.

examples.title: Federation: where are these books held? (via USTC)
examples.tip: A CROSS-SOURCE join from the other side: pre-loads the USTC catalogue as a second source. Each Embassy book links rdfs:seeAlso -> its USTC edition; the query follows that into USTC to list the libraries that hold a physical copy (Herzog August, BSB, British Library...) and the printer. Remove the ustc chip to query the Embassy alone.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX u: <https://www.ustc.ac.uk/ontology#>
SELECT ?title ?printer ?library WHERE {
  ?book a schema:Book ; rdfs:label ?title ; rdfs:seeAlso ?ed .
  ?ed u:printer ?p . ?p rdfs:label ?printer .
  ?ed u:heldBy ?l . ?l rdfs:label ?library
}
LIMIT 40

examples.title: What's in the collection
examples.tip: The shape of the graph at a glance: 2,307 hermetic/esoteric Books, 764,708 Pages (each a scanned page image), 991 authors (schema:Person), 725 geocoded Places and ~127k subject/category/collection Concepts. One count per rdf:type.

examples.title: Alchemy books (with cover images)
examples.tip: Books filed under the 'alchemy' subject category, oldest first, each with author, year and its cover thumbnail (the -thumb.jpg renders inline). Swap the category IRI for /kabbalah, /rosicrucianism, /mysticism, /astrology or /medicine to browse another shelf.

examples.title: Books by language
examples.tip: The library is deeply multilingual: German (929) and Latin (585) dominate, then English, French, Dutch, Italian, Hebrew and more. Count of books per dct:language.

examples.title: The oldest books in the library

examples.tip: The AI-inferred related-works links (efmo:relatedBook) as a node-link graph - each book joined to the titles it is connected to (citations, influences, same-work editions). A small influence neighbourhood of the collection.

datasets.label: USTC - Universal Short Title Catalogue (727 Embassy/BPH-cited editions, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: A bounded, federation-ready extract of the Universal Short Title Catalogue (ustc.ac.uk, University of St Andrews) - the authoritative bibliography of early-modern European print. Exactly the 727 editions the Embassy of the Free Mind / BPH collection cites (by USTC number), harvested from the public edition pages as a FAIR-USE research subset: USTC is a copyrighted scholarly database with no open licence and no bulk API, so this is 727 of ~1M records - NOT a copy of the catalogue (© USTC / University of St Andrews). Each edition (ustc:Edition, IRI = https://www.ustc.ac.uk/editions/{sn}) carries its standardized title, imprint, place/country/region, year, format (2°/4°/8°/12°...), pagination, authors (with roles) and printers (Lukas Jennis, Lazarus Zetzner's heirs and the other great alchemical presses), USTC classifications (Religious, Science, Medical, Philosophy, Witchcraft & Demonology...), language(s) (Latin, German, French, Dutch, English, Greek, Hebrew), 10,779 library HOLDINGS across 1,146 institutions (Herzog August Bibliothek Wolfenbüttel, British Library, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, SBB Berlin...) each with shelfmark, and 891 links to DIGITAL copies (Google Books, ProQuest EEB, Cervantes Virtual...). 88,452 triples, remote-lazy. Built to FEDERATE with the bph dataset - the edition IRI is exactly bph's rdfs:seeAlso target and every edition back-links u:embassyBook -> the Embassy book, so one cross-source query joins the Embassy's cover + AI summary to USTC's imprint, printers and library holdings. schema.org / Dublin Core / SKOS. Attribute USTC / University of St Andrews.
datasets.license: © USTC / Univ. of St Andrews (research subset)

examples.title: Digitised editions — cover + IIIF
examples.tip: USTC hosts no images itself, but ~40% of these editions link to a digitised copy at an open IIIF library (Bavarian State Library / MDZ, Gallica, ONB Austria, Google Books). A cover thumbnail is resolved deterministically from that link (schema:image, renders inline) plus a link to the full IIIF manifest — here the Rosicrucian, Kabbalah and Hermetic title-pages. Providers like ProQuest/EEBO are subscription-gated, so they stay as plain out-links.

examples.title: What's in this USTC subset
examples.tip: The shape of the extract: 727 early-modern Editions, 10,779 library Copies (physical holdings), 1,146 Libraries, and ~1,226 Persons (authors + printers). One count per rdf:type. This is only the 727 editions the Embassy/BPH collection cites - a fair-use slice of USTC's ~1M records.

examples.title: Which libraries hold these books
examples.tip: Counts holdings per library (by institution + city, so same-named 'Universitätsbibliothek' entries stay distinct). The great early-modern collections surface: Herzog August Bibliothek (Wolfenbüttel), the British Library, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek (München), Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX u: <https://www.ustc.ac.uk/ontology#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?library ?city (COUNT(?e) AS ?editions) WHERE {
  ?e u:heldBy ?l . ?l rdfs:label ?library ; u:city ?city
}
GROUP BY ?l ?library ?city
ORDER BY DESC(?editions)
LIMIT 25

examples.title: Books by USTC classification
examples.tip: The subject make-up of the Embassy's cited editions in USTC's own classification scheme - Religious (313), Science, Medical Texts, Philosophy and Morality, and the tell-tale 'Witchcraft and Demonology'. Count of editions per dcterms:subject.

PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
SELECT ?classification (COUNT(?e) AS ?editions) WHERE {
  ?e dct:subject ?c . ?c skos:prefLabel ?classification
}
GROUP BY ?classification
ORDER BY DESC(?editions)

examples.title: Editions with a digital copy
examples.tip: USTC records where a digitisation is available online - the title plus the deep link (Google Books, ProQuest Early European Books, Cervantes Virtual...). 514 of the 727 editions have at least one. The URL column is clickable.

examples.title: The busiest printers
examples.tip: Editions per printer/press (skipping 's.n.' = sine nomine, printer unknown). This is a who's-who of the early-modern alchemical trade: Lukas Jennis and the heirs of Lazarus Zetzner (both Frankfurt/Strasbourg) printed much of the Rosicrucian and Hermetic corpus.

examples.title: The oldest editions
examples.tip: Sorted by year ascending - the earliest imprints in the Embassy's cited set, each with its place of printing and format (2° folio, 4° quarto, 8° octavo...). schema:datePublished is a typed xsd:gYear.

examples.title: Federation: Embassy cover ⋈ USTC record
examples.tip: A CROSS-SOURCE join. This pre-loads the bph (Embassy of the Free Mind) graph as a second source (see the Sources strip). Each USTC edition back-links u:embassyBook -> the Embassy book; the query then pulls that book's cover image + AI summary from bph and shows them beside USTC's imprint and place - two catalogues describing the same physical book, joined on the shared identity. Remove the bph chip to query USTC alone.

datasets.label: Fuero Juzgo — the manuscript tradition: 52 witnesses, IIIF, Wikidata & Biblissima (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The manuscript tradition of the FUERO JUZGO — the 13th-century Romance (Castilian / Leonese / Asturian) translation of the Visigothic Liber Iudiciorum, made c. 1260 under Fernando III. Compiled from Mónica Castillo Lluch's Índice de fueros (UNIL) and PhiloBiblon (BETA, texid 1191): all 46 PhiloBiblon witnesses + the Galician López Ferreiro fragment + 3 BOOST-only manuscripts + 2 twelfth-century Catalan fragments of the Libre jutge = 52 testimonies, each with shelfmark (fjo:siglum), holding institution, dialect (leonés occidental/oriental, asturiano, castellano, agallegado…), an integer date range (fjo:notBefore/notAfter, so you can query 'all 13th-c. witnesses'), PhiloBiblon manid/anaid, and — where recorded — its incipit, prologue incipit, explicit and scribal colophon (the shared prologue 'Con cuidado del amor de Cristo… de don Sisnando' and the 'Pedro Martiz Gualego me scripso' colophon thread through the tradition). The manuscript STEMMA is modelled (fjo:copyOf links the 18th-c. antiquarian copies BNE 683 & 1681 back to their medieval exemplars — the Códice Murciano, Escorial d.III.18 & P.II.17). 12 EDITIONS (Villadiego 1600 → Llorente 1792 → Reguera 1798 → the RAE 1815[1817] academic edition promoted by Jovellanos → Orazi, Perona, Romero Cambrón…) link by fjo:editsWitness to the exact codices they establish; 11 STUDIES (Menéndez Pidal, Gessner, Fernández Llera, Castillo Lluch, García Martín…) link by fjo:studies. 12 DIGITIZED witnesses carry a IIIF manifest (fjo:iiifManifest) that renders as an in-table facsimile viewer — both Munich BSB codices, the BnF Espagnol 256 (Gallica), the Bodleian Holkham misc. 46 and all 8 Escorial codices (Real Biblioteca Digital); the flagship is BSB Cod.hisp. 28 (365 canvases, CC Public Domain Mark). Works, institutions, persons and places carry owl:sameAs to Wikidata (so the graph FEDERATES with the wikidata datasets and, via the cross-source join, with live Wikidata — see the map example), and two witnesses are owl:sameAs Biblissima+ entities (BnF Esp. 256 = Q44277, BSB Cod.hisp. 6 = Q264558), bridging to the `biblissima` dataset. A small purpose-built ontology (fjo:, Work/Witness/Edition/Study/Person/Institution/Place, aligned to Dublin Core, FOAF, SKOS, schema.org) travels inside the file. ~1.5k triples, remote-lazy over HTTP range (served from Cloudflare R2, data.graphplaza.com). Built by scripts/fuero_juzgo_to_nt.py from the two curated sources + verified IIIF/Wikidata/Biblissima lookups — no scraping. Scholarly compilation; credit Mónica Castillo Lluch (Índice de fueros, UNIL) and PhiloBiblon; BSB Cod.hisp. 28 images CC PDM 1.0.

examples.title: What's in this corpus
examples.tip:
The shape of the Fuero Juzgo dataset, counted by fjo: class: 49 Manuscripts + 3 Fragments (the 46 PhiloBiblon witnesses, the Galician López Ferreiro fragment, 3 BOOST-only mss and the 2 Catalan Libre-jutge fragments), 12 Editions, 11 Studies, 3 Works (the Fuero Juzgo, its Latin source the Liber Iudiciorum, and the Catalan Libre jutge), plus the People, Institutions and Places that link them.
One row per class.

examples.title: 📜 Manuscripts you can SEE (IIIF facsimiles)
examples.tip:
The 12 digitized witnesses that carry a IIIF manifest (fjo:iiifManifest): both Munich BSB codices (Cod.hisp. 28 & 6), the BnF Espagnol 256 (Gallica), the Bodleian Holkham misc. 46, and all 8 Escorial codices (Real Biblioteca Digital). The Facsimile column (fjo:image) renders a folio inline; click a IIIF cell for the page-turning viewer.
Every facsimile is MIRRORED into our own R2 (all 3,223 full-res pages under fuero_juzgo/iiif/) with a self-hosted IIIF manifest, so it renders and downloads without depending on the source servers; fjo:sourceManifest keeps a link to the original. BSB Cod.hisp. 28 is CC Public Domain Mark.

examples.title: The tradition over time (witnesses per century)
examples.tip:
Every witness carries an integer date range (fjo:notBefore / fjo:notAfter), so fjo:century buckets the 52 testimonies: 2 in the 12th c. (the Catalan fragments), 26 in the 13th (the core of the surviving tradition, copied within a generation of the c. 1260 translation), 11 in the 14th, then a long tail of late copies down to the 18th-c. antiquarian apographs.
Switch Output to a bar chart to see the 13th-century peak.

examples.title: The oldest witnesses & their dialect
examples.tip:
The 13th-century-or-earlier witnesses, with the linguistic characterisation editors give them (fjo:languageVariety): the tradition is a dialect map of the medieval north-west - leonés occidental / centro-occidental / oriental, asturiano (the Munich Cod.hisp. 28), and castellano. The Códice Murciano (1288) is castellano copied from a strongly Leonese model.
Sorted earliest-first; 'Held by' is the current holding library.

examples.title: The manuscript stemma (copies of copies)
examples.tip:
fjo:copyOf reconstructs the transmission: the 18th-century antiquarian copies made for the RAE academic edition trace back to their medieval exemplars - BNE 683 (Santiago y Palomares, 1755, corrected by the Jesuit Burriel) is a copy of the Códice Murciano (1288), and BNE 1681 (1762-64) copies the Escorial codices P.II.17 and d.III.18.
Three copy-of links; the exemplar is always centuries older than the copy.

examples.title: Critical editions ↔ the codices they establish
examples.tip:
fjo:editsWitness links each modern edition to the exact manuscript it edits: Mencé-Caster (1996) -> Escorial Z.III.6, Orazi (1997) -> Z.III.21, Perona et al. (2002) -> the Códice Murciano, Romero Cambrón (2016) -> the Bodleian Holkham misc. 46, and the RAE academic edition (1815, really 1817) collates three Escorial codices (Z.III.18, M.II.18, d.III.18).
The scholarly editions, joined to their base witnesses.

PREFIX fjo: <https://w3id.org/fuero-juzgo/ontology#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?edition ?codex ?shelf WHERE {
  ?ed fjo:editsWitness ?w ; rdfs:label ?edition .
  ?w rdfs:label ?codex ; fjo:siglum ?shelf .
}
ORDER BY ?edition

examples.title: Search the prologues & colophons
examples.tip:
Full-text search (backed by the .rete text index) over the incipits, prologues and scribal colophons transcribed from PhiloBiblon. Here, the witnesses whose prologue names King Sisenando (the Visigothic king in whose reign the IV Council of Toledo met, invoked at the head of the code) - the shared 'Con cuidado del amor de Cristo... de don Sisnando' opening that threads through the tradition.

examples.title: 🔗 Linked out: witnesses also in Biblissima

Two witnesses carry owl:sameAs into Biblissima+ (data.biblissima.fr), the French manuscript-and-IIIF aggregator: the BnF Espagnol 256 (Q44277) and the Munich BSB Cod.hisp. 6 (Q264558). PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?witness ?biblissima ?iiif WHERE {
  ?w owl:sameAs ?biblissima ; fjo:iiifManifest ?iiif ; rdfs:label ?witness .
  FILTER(STRSTARTS(STR(?biblissima), "https://data.biblissima.fr/"))
}

examples.title: Cross-source JOIN: the libraries' countries (live Wikidata)
examples.tip:
ONE query split across TWO sources and joined on the shared ?wd. This file answers 'which library holds a witness' and gives it an owl:sameAs Wikidata id; LIVE Wikidata answers wdt:P17 (the library's country). The playground routes each pattern to the source that can answer it, then bound-joins - so you see the international diaspora of the tradition's custodians (Germany, France, Spain, United Kingdom, United States, Sweden, Denmark, Portugal).

datasets.label: BVPB - Ramón Llull: 142 digitised editions & manuscripts (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The complete Ramón Llull collection of the Biblioteca Virtual del Patrimonio Bibliográfico (BVPB, Spanish Ministry of Culture): 142 digitised works by the Mallorcan polymath Ramón Llull (Doctor Illuminatus, ca. 1232-1315) - manuscripts and early printed editions (14th-18th c.) of the Ars, Arbor Scientiae, Ars Brevis, Ars generalis ultima, the Liber magnus contemplationis in Deum and the rest of the Lullian corpus, in Latin, Catalan and Castilian. Each work is an edm:ProvidedCHO carrying full Dublin Core - title, creator/contributor, date, publisher & place of printing, language, subject, physical description (dc:format), coverage and rights - plus its BVPB control number, edm:isShownAt (the catalogue landing page), edm:isShownBy (the whole digitised object as a single PDF, served from bvpb.mcu.es) and foaf:page (the page-image viewer). The 71 PRINTED editions are additionally FULL-TEXT SEARCHABLE: every one was OCR'd page by page (Tesseract lat + a dictionary-guided long-ſ correction that turns 'fapientia' back into 'sapientia'), ~8.7M words held as bvpb:fulltext and backed by the .rete text index, and given a IIIF v3 manifest (bvpb:iiifManifest) that opens a page-turning viewer with the OCR word layer over the facsimile - try the '🔎 Full-text search' and '📖 IIIF viewers' examples. Manuscripts are metadata-only (Tesseract can't read the hands - that needs HTR). 2,877 triples (25.7 MB with the text layer), remote-lazy over HTTP range. Harvested from the BVPB Ramón Llull microsite by scripts/bvpb_ramonllull.py, modelled by scripts/bvpb_to_nt.py, OCR/IIIF by scripts/bvpb_ocr_iiif.py. CC BY 4.0 - credit the Biblioteca Virtual del Patrimonio Bibliográfico (Ministerio de Cultura, España). Shares the early-modern rare-book domain with the bph and ustc collections.

examples.title: What's in this collection
examples.tip:
The shape of the BVPB Ramón Llull collection: 142 digitised works, split by dc:type into 'Manuscritos' (hand-written medieval codices) and 'Libros' (early printed editions, 15th-18th c.).
One count per Dublin Core type - the manuscripts are the older, rarer half of the Lullian corpus here.

examples.title: Languages of the Lullian corpus
examples.tip:
Works per language (dc:language, ISO 639-2 codes): 'lat' = Latin (the bulk of Llull's scholastic output), 'cat' = Catalan (his own vernacular, which he pioneered for philosophy), 'spa' = Castilian.
Ramón Llull wrote across all three, and the collection reflects it.

examples.title: Read the books: every work + its PDF
examples.tip:
Each work with its date and edm:isShownBy - the whole digitised object as a single PDF served from bvpb.mcu.es. The PDF column is a clickable link (the 142 PDFs are ~13 GB in total).
Sorted oldest-first, so the 14th-15th-century manuscripts (e.g. the Ars demonstrativa, Arbor Scientiae) lead.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX dc: <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/>
PREFIX edm: <http://www.europeana.eu/schemas/edm/>
SELECT ?title ?date ?pdf WHERE {
  ?s dc:title ?title ; dc:date ?date ; edm:isShownBy ?pdf .
}
ORDER BY ?date
LIMIT 50

examples.title: The printers & publishers
examples.tip:
Editions per publisher/printer (dc:publisher). The early-modern Mallorca presses surface - the house of the Viuda de Guasp and Typis Viduae Frau (Palma de Mallorca) printed much of the 17th-18th-century Lullian revival.
Manuscripts have no publisher, so this counts only the printed editions.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX dc: <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/>
SELECT ?publisher (COUNT(?s) AS ?works) WHERE {
  ?s dc:publisher ?publisher
}
GROUP BY ?publisher
ORDER BY DESC(?works)
LIMIT 25

examples.title: The manuscripts, with their physical description
examples.tip:
Just the hand-written codices (dc:type = 'Manuscritos'): each with its date and dc:format - the codicological description (number of leaves, parchment vs paper, columns, dimensions in cm).
These are the medieval witnesses of Llull's text, the scholarly heart of the collection.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX dc: <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/>
SELECT ?title ?date ?format WHERE {
  ?s dc:type ?type ; dc:title ?title ; dc:date ?date ; dc:format ?format .
  FILTER(STR(?type) = "Manuscritos")
}
ORDER BY ?date
LIMIT 40

examples.title: 🔎 Full-text search across the OCR'd books
examples.tip:
Full-text search over the OCR of all 71 PRINTED editions (Tesseract lat + dictionary long-ſ repair, ~8.7M words held as bvpb:fulltext, backed by the .rete text index). This finds every book whose pages mention 'sapientia' (wisdom) - change the term to search the whole corpus.
The Open (IIIF) column opens the page-turning facsimile with the OCR word layer; the OCR is an automatic scaffold, not a critical edition. NOTE a FILTER(CONTAINS) scans the fulltext (~19 MB fetched), so give it a moment; enable Settings → Range cache to make re-runs instant.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX bvpb: <https://bvpb.mcu.es/ns#>
PREFIX dc: <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/>
SELECT ?title ?date ?manifest WHERE {
  ?s bvpb:fulltext ?txt ; dc:title ?title ; dc:date ?date ; bvpb:iiifManifest ?manifest .
  FILTER(CONTAINS(LCASE(STR(?txt)), "sapientia"))
}
LIMIT 25

examples.title: 📖 Page-turning IIIF viewers (printed editions)
examples.tip:
The 71 printed editions, each with a IIIF v3 manifest (bvpb:iiifManifest) - click a ?manifest cell to open the page-turning viewer (facsimile images served from R2 + the OCR word layer). Sorted by page count; the Operum Tomus volumes run past 1,000 pages.
Manuscripts are absent here - Tesseract can't read the hands, which would need HTR (Transkribus / eScriptorium).
examples.sparql:
PREFIX bvpb: <https://bvpb.mcu.es/ns#>
PREFIX dc: <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/>
SELECT ?title ?pages ?manifest WHERE {
  ?s bvpb:iiifManifest ?manifest ; dc:title ?title ; bvpb:pageCount ?pages .
}
ORDER BY DESC(?pages)
LIMIT 30

datasets.label: BOE — Legislación Consolidada: every in-force Spanish law (12,330) as an ELI citation graph (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The ENTIRE consolidated-legislation corpus of Spain's Boletín Oficial del Estado — every actively-maintained norm in force (State + the autonomous communities + the foral regimes), 12,330 in all, as a European-Legislation-Identifier (ELI) knowledge graph. Each norm sits at its REAL canonical ELI IRI (https://www.boe.es/eli/es/l/2015/10/01/40 = Ley 40/2015 de Régimen Jurídico del Sector Público), typed eli:LegalResource and by its rango (bx:Ley, bx:LeyOrganica, bx:RealDecreto, bx:RealDecretoLey, bx:Orden, bx:Reglamento… — 19 classes rdfs:subClassOf eli:LegalResource, so `rete`'s type-pyramid communities ARE the kinds of norm), carrying eli:title, eli:id_local (the BOE-A-… identifier), eli:number, eli:date_document / date_publication / first_date_entry_in_force (typed xsd:date), eli:passed_by → its issuing department (149 organisations — Jefatura del Estado & the ministries + the CCAA governments), eli:jurisdiction (Estatal/Autonómico) and eli:is_about → its subjects (drawn from the BOE's 6,829-term SKOS materia thesaurus). The heart of it is the NORM-TO-NORM CITATION / DEROGATION NETWORK mined from the BOE's own análisis: ~100,000 edges typed with the STANDARD ELI relations — eli:repeals (deroga, 19.5k), eli:amends (modifica, 32.9k), eli:corrects (corrige), eli:cites, eli:transposes (1,042 EU-directive transpositions), eli:based_on (dictada en virtud de) — plus a small bx: extension for BOE-specific acts (publishes / approves / authorizes / ratifies / challenges / declares / interprets). So you can ask which laws have been reformed most (the Ley de Demarcación y Planta Judicial — 134 amendments; the IRPF and IVA tax codes; the Ley de Enjuiciamiento Civil), what the 1978 Constitution repealed (the Franco-era Leyes Fundamentales: the Ley de Sucesión en la Jefatura del Estado, the Fuero de los Españoles, the Ley Orgánica del Estado, the Ley 1/1977 de Reforma Política…), or which norms have been most challenged before the Constitutional Court (the Código Penal — 51 recursos/cuestiones). Referenced norms outside the in-force set (already-repealed or pre-consolidation, including Gaceta-era laws back to the 19th c.) become 28,796 lightweight labelled nodes so no derogation edge dangles. A full-text index over all 41k titles finds every norm on 'inteligencia artificial', 'cambio climático' or 'protección de datos'. 465k triples, 7.9 MB, remote-lazy over HTTP range on Cloudflare R2. Built from the OFFICIAL BOE Open-Data API (the legislación-consolidada enumeration + a per-norm /análisis call + the /datos-auxiliares controlled vocabularies) by scripts/boe_to_nt.py — no scraping. Because the norms carry real ELI IRIs and the ELI ontology, the graph federates with EUR-Lex and the other national ELI publishers. Reuse under Ley 37/2007 + the BOE standard reuse licence (Resolución 27-jun-2024): credit 'Basado en datos de la Agencia Estatal Boletín Oficial del Estado'.

examples.title: 🧠 Every norm with the force of law — reasoning over the taxonomy
examples.tip:
The rango classes now form a two-tier ontology: bx:NormaConRangoDeLey groups the force-of-law kinds (Ley, Ley Orgánica, Decreto Legislativo, Decreto-ley…) and bx:NormaReglamentaria the regulatory ones (Real Decreto, Orden, Resolución…), both under eli:LegalResource.
NO norm is typed with the intermediate class directly, so with 🧠 Reason OFF this returns 0 rows. Turn it ON and OWL 2 QL rewrites `a bx:NormaConRangoDeLey` along rdfs:subClassOf, returning all 4,967 norms with the force of law. Flip Reason off to see the difference.

examples.title: 🧠 What has amended this law? — inverse reasoning
examples.tip:
The amendment network stores only the forward edge: X eli:amends Y. The ontology declares bx:amendedBy owl:inverseOf eli:amends, so the reverse edges are NOT stored — they're entailed.
With 🧠 Reason ON, asking what amended the Ley 38/1988 de Demarcación y de Planta Judicial (the most-reformed law in force — its judicial map redrawn with every new court) returns all 134 amending norms by reversing the eli:amends edges. Reason OFF → 0 rows. Swap the IRI for any norm.

examples.title: ★ The living laws — most-reformed norms in force
examples.tip: eli:amends is the 'modifica' relation mined from the BOE's own análisis, so counting the INCOMING amendments ranks the most-reformed laws still in force. Top is the Ley 38/1988 de Demarcación y de Planta Judicial (134 reforms — the judicial map is redrawn every time a court is added), then the great tax codes (IRPF — Ley 35/2006; IVA — Ley 37/1992; Impuestos Especiales), the texto refundido de la Ley General de la Seguridad Social, the Ley 1/2000 de Enjuiciamiento Civil and the Ley Orgánica 6/1985 del Poder Judicial. These are the laws Parliament keeps touching.

examples.title: What the 1978 Constitution repealed
examples.tip: The Constitución Española (its ELI work IRI is es/c/1978/12/27) sits at the top of the hierarchy of norms — and here is what it swept away. Its disposición derogatoria repeals the Franco-era Leyes Fundamentales del Reino: the Ley de Sucesión en la Jefatura del Estado (1947), the Ley reguladora del Fuero de los Españoles (1945), the Ley Orgánica del Estado (1967), the Ley de Principios del Movimiento Nacional (1958) and the Ley 1/1977 para la Reforma Política that dissolved the regime. The transition to democracy, as eli:repeals edges.

examples.title: Most challenged before the Constitutional Court
examples.tip: bx:challenges gathers the recursos and cuestiones de inconstitucionalidad and conflictos raised against a norm (BOE análisis relation codes 520/530/552/694). The most-contested law in force is the Ley Orgánica 10/1995 del Código Penal (51 challenges), then the Ley 24/1983 de saneamiento de las Haciendas Locales and the Real Decreto-ley 28/2012 on the Seguridad Social pension freeze — the fault lines of Spanish constitutional litigation.

examples.title: Search: laws on artificial intelligence
examples.tip: Full-text search over the 41k norm titles (a rete text index backs CONTAINS). 'Inteligencia artificial' surfaces the Real Decreto 729/2023 that created AESIA — the Agencia Española de Supervisión de Inteligencia Artificial, the first such national supervisor in the EU — and Extremadura's Decreto-ley 2/2023. Swap the phrase for 'cambio climático', 'protección de datos', 'memoria democrática', 'vivienda' or any ministry's name.

examples.title: Reforms of the Código Penal, as a network
examples.tip: Switch Output to Graph. The node-link neighbourhood of ONE norm — the Código Penal (Ley Orgánica 10/1995) — with every law that has amended it fanning out from the centre (eli:amends), 43 reforms in all: the 2015 overhaul, the LO 4/2023 on delitos contra la libertad sexual ('sólo sí es sí'), the LO 1/2024 de amnistía… Change the central IRI to es/l/2000/01/07/1 (Enjuiciamiento Civil) or es/lo/1985/07/01/6 (Poder Judicial) to map another law's reform history.

examples.title: Legislative output, year by year
examples.tip: Switch Output to Time. The norms in force counted by their year of adoption (eli:date_document) — the shape of the currently-live statute book over time. It climbs through the 2000s and 2010s and spikes in 2020 (795 norms — the COVID-19 emergency legislation). Older law is thinner because superseded norms have dropped out of the consolidated set.

datasets.label: bcul.rete — BCU Lausanne: a digital twin of the whole library, incl. where every book is held (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: A range-queryable graph twin of the Bibliothèque cantonale et universitaire de Lausanne, aggregating four of its public interfaces into one 117.5M-triple graph. The ENTIRE Renouvaud catalogue — 3.55M bibliographic records mirrored from the Alma SRU endpoint of the Vaud library network (zone 41BCULAUSA_LIB) — carries full physical HOLDINGS: every book resolves to WHICH library holds it (BCUL sites Unithèque / Riponne / Internef, the Archives cantonales vaudoises, the Musée des beaux-arts, and dozens of faculty, gymnasium and municipal libraries), its shelving location, call number and live availability (available / unavailable / check_holdings) via 4.9M b:heldAt edges to shared Library nodes. Plus the Patrinum digital-heritage repository (332k digitized books, archives, iconography, Fonds Roud, Personnalités Vaudoises — OAI-PMH), the 15 medieval manuscripts BCUL has on e-codices (IIIF + TEI + DOI), and 331 digitized-press titles from Scriptorium (24 Heures & the Feuille d'avis de Lausanne back to 1762). Modelled with schema.org + Dublin Core and connected through 2.7M author/agent nodes, 2.44M subject concepts, places and the Library nodes; 334k items link to a digitized thumbnail, 15 to a IIIF manifest. Harvested entirely from the library's public APIs (no scraping); rights vary per source (dcterms:rights per record). Engineering: Alma SRU caps every query at 10,000 records → a recursive mms_id-space bisection (594 leaves) yields a provably-complete mirror; ~3s SRU latency → a 12-way concurrent harvest.

datasets.label: GBIF Birds — Spain & Switzerland: 50M sightings with a taxonomic zoom + map (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: Fifty MILLION georeferenced bird (Aves) occurrences — Spain 47.9M, Switzerland 2.26M, 1,104 species — from the GBIF Open Data snapshot (2026-07-01), as one 334M-triple range-queryable file (1.53 GB, remote-lazy over HTTP range). This is the SEMANTIC-ZOOM dataset: every occurrence is rdf:type its species, and each species carries a full taxonomic subClassOf chain Species ⊑ Genus ⊑ Family ⊑ Order ⊑ Aves ⊑ Chordata ⊑ Animalia — so the schema pyramid rolls the 50M sightings up into a 6-LEVEL zoom you can read WITHOUT touching the triple index (open the Schema tab): level 3 = Orders (Passeriformes 29.7M, Charadriiformes 5.1M, Accipitriformes/raptors 2.9M, Anseriformes 2.2M …), level 4 = Families (Fringillidae, Muscicapidae, Accipitridae, Laridae …), level 5 = the 1,104 species. Ask a question about birds at the Order or Family level and you never descend to a single record — the abstraction is the point. ENRICHED build: every species now also carries its COMMON NAME in up to 47 European languages (27,922 language-tagged dwc:vernacularName — French, Catalan, Basque, Welsh, Breton … all present), its IUCN Red List category (967 species; 165 flagged v:sensitive as near-threatened or worse), and precomputed occurrence stats (recordCount, estimatedIndividuals, first/last year). And it is an RDF-STAR showcase: each ADDED fact is a quoted triple annotated with its provenance — << species dwc:vernacularName '…' >> dct:source 'Catalogue of Life' ; prov:generatedAtTime '2026-07-11' — statements about statements, the natural home for who-said-it-and-when. Every occurrence also carries a GeoSPARQL POINT (map view), its country, year, basis-of-record (mostly citizen-science HUMAN_OBSERVATION — eBird & friends), source dataset and its dwc:individualCount where the observer recorded one (33.4M records). IRIs round-trip to live GBIF: occurrence = gbif.org/occurrence/<id>, species owl:sameAs gbif.org/species/<key>. Built KEYLESS from the GBIF AWS Parquet snapshot via DuckDB (scripts/gbif_birds_extract.py + gbif_birds_to_nt.py); names from the GBIF vernacular API, conservation from the IUCN Red List via Wikidata; enrichment emitted as N-Triples-star (scripts/gbif_birds_enrich_nt.py). CC BY-NC 4.0 (GBIF); cite GBIF.org. Selective queries (a species, a small area), the Schema pyramid, and every enrichment lookup are cheap over HTTP range; a full 50M-row aggregate scans the file, so lean on the pyramid for the big picture.

examples.title: ★ Semantic zoom: the taxonomic ladder of a species
examples.tip:
The whole point of this dataset. rdfs:subClassOf+ walks the Barn Swallow (Hirundo rustica) UP its taxonomic ladder: Genus Hirundo → Family Hirundinidae → Order Passeriformes → Class Aves → Phylum Chordata → Kingdom Animalia. This same chain, over all 1,104 species, is what the Schema tab rolls the 50M sightings up into — open it to see the 6-level pyramid (level 3 = Orders: Passeriformes 29.7M, raptors 2.9M …).
Ask a bird question at the Order or Family level and you never touch a single record. Swap the species key (owl:sameAs gbif.org/species/<key>) for any of the 1,104.
