PREFIX dwc: <http://rs.tdwg.org/dwc/terms/>
PREFIX v: <https://w3id.org/rete/gbif/vocab#>
SELECT ?rank ?name WHERE {
  <https://w3id.org/rete/gbif/taxon/species/9515886> rdfs:subClassOf+ ?anc .
  ?anc rdfs:label ?name ; dwc:taxonRank ?rank .
}

examples.title: ✨ RDF-star: where did this name come from?
examples.tip:
The headline of this build — provenance as RDF-star. Each name assertion is itself a QUOTED TRIPLE << species dwc:vernacularName "…" >> annotated with dct:source (which checklist it came from) and prov:generatedAtTime (when we added it). Here: every name of the Egyptian Vulture (Neophron percnopterus, IUCN Endangered) with its source — fr 'Petit vautour', ca 'Miloca', es 'Alimoche'.
This is a statement ABOUT a statement: the name has no node of its own, so the provenance lives on the quoted triple. Add `prov:wasDerivedFrom ?api` to get the live GBIF API URL each name was pulled from.

PREFIX dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/>
PREFIX prov: <http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#>
SELECT ?name ?src ?when WHERE {
  << <https://w3id.org/rete/gbif/taxon/species/2480696> dwc:vernacularName ?name >>
     dct:source ?src ; prov:generatedAtTime ?when .
}

examples.tip:
A taxonomy-driven map: all occurrences whose species is (transitively) in the hawk-and-eagle family Accipitridae — hitting the pyramid's Family level, then joining to points. This crosses the taxonomy INTO the geography. Heavier than a single-species map (it fans out over many species), so it's LIMITed; give it a moment on a cold cache.
This is the 'ask at the Family level, get a map' pattern — no need to name every eagle and harrier species.

examples.title: One sighting, the full record
examples.tip:
Everything the graph knows about a single occurrence — its species type, GeoSPARQL point, country, year, basis-of-record and source dataset. The subject IRI is the live GBIF occurrence page.
Swap the occurrence IRI for any ?occ you get from the other examples.

examples.title: Taxonomic richness: which genera have the most species?
examples.tip:
A pure-taxonomy question, answered over the small T-Box (the ~13k subClassOf/label triples) — NOT the 50M records, so it's cheap. Counts how many species each genus contains: Emberiza (buntings) 21, Anas (dabbling ducks) 18, Calidris (sandpipers) 18, Sylvia (typical warblers) 18 … the most speciose bird genera recorded in Spain + Switzerland.
This is the ontology talking, not the observations — the pyramid's raw material.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX dwc: <http://rs.tdwg.org/dwc/terms/>
PREFIX v: <https://w3id.org/rete/gbif/vocab#>
SELECT ?genus (COUNT(?sp) AS ?n) WHERE {
  ?sp dwc:taxonRank "species" ; rdfs:subClassOf ?g .
  ?g rdfs:label ?genus ; dwc:taxonRank "genus" .
}
GROUP BY ?genus ORDER BY DESC(?n) LIMIT 25

examples.title: 🗺️ Map the Bearded Vulture — Alps ↔ Pyrenees
examples.tip:
The Bearded Vulture (Gypaetus barbatus, gbif.org/species/2480649) — one of Europe's rarest raptors, its bone-eating lammergeier — maps beautifully across BOTH countries: a native Pyrenean stronghold in Spain and the famous Alpine reintroduction in Switzerland. Bounded to one species, so it's a cheap lazy map.
Try 2481912 (White Stork), 4352332 (Greater Flamingo), 2481047 (Peregrine Falcon) for other icons.

examples.title: 📈 White Stork sightings by year
examples.tip:
The White Stork (Ciconia ciconia) recorded per year — switch Output to Time to see the curve. Bounded to one species, and the count climbs steeply with the rise of citizen-science checklists (~52k in 2024). A window onto observer effort as much as bird numbers.
Swap the species key to chart any bird's recording history; the low current-year bar is just the year-to-date.

examples.title: How is a species recorded? (basis of record)
examples.tip:
Where the data comes from, for one species (Blue Tit, Cyanistes caeruleus): HUMAN_OBSERVATION (a birdwatcher's checklist) dwarfs PRESERVED_SPECIMEN (a museum skin), LIVING_SPECIMEN (a ringed/zoo bird) and MACHINE_OBSERVATION (a camera/acoustic sensor). Bird data is overwhelmingly citizen science.
Museum-heavy groups look very different — try an insect or a plant species in the full-taxa build if we ship one.

examples.title: 🗺️ Map a whole genus: the falcons (Falco)
examples.tip:
Taxonomy → geography at the GENUS level: every falcon (genus Falco — Kestrel, Peregrine, Hobby, Merlin, Eleonora's …) mapped in one query via rdfs:subClassOf+, no need to name each species. Fans out over several species, so it's LIMITed and a touch heavier than a single-species map.
Swap /genus/Falco for /genus/Aquila (true eagles), /genus/Larus (large gulls), /genus/Anas (dabbling ducks).

examples.title: The bird orders, by species richness
examples.tip:
Every bird Order and how many species it holds, over the T-Box only (cheap): the perching birds Passeriformes dominate with 410 species, then Charadriiformes (waders & gulls) 148, Anseriformes (wildfowl) 123 — and Psittaciformes (parrots) 60, a telltale sign of escaped/feral cage-birds now breeding in Spain (Monk & Rose-ringed Parakeets).
This is level 3 of the schema pyramid as a query; the Schema tab shows the same rollup weighted by sightings instead of species.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX dwc: <http://rs.tdwg.org/dwc/terms/>
PREFIX v: <https://w3id.org/rete/gbif/vocab#>
SELECT ?order (COUNT(DISTINCT ?sp) AS ?n) WHERE {
  ?sp dwc:taxonRank "species" ; rdfs:subClassOf+ ?o .
  ?o dwc:taxonRank "order" ; rdfs:label ?order .
}
GROUP BY ?order ORDER BY DESC(?n)

examples.title: Genera in a family: the ducks & geese (Anatidae)
examples.tip:
One step of the taxonomy: the genera directly inside family Anatidae (wildfowl) — Aix, Anas (dabbling ducks), Anser (grey geese), Aythya (diving ducks), Branta, Mergus, Tadorna … the shape of a family at a glance.
Swap /family/Anatidae for /family/Muscicapidae (chats & flycatchers), /family/Laridae (gulls), /family/Fringillidae (finches).

examples.title: 🗺️ Flamingos in Spain (Doñana, Ebro delta, Fuente de Piedra)
examples.tip:
A species map narrowed to ONE country: Greater Flamingo (Phoenicopterus roseus) sightings in Spain only — the great saline wetlands light up (the Guadalquivir marshes at Doñana, the Ebro delta, the Fuente de Piedra lagoon). Bounded by species AND v:inCountry, so it's a cheap, targeted lazy read.
Switch the country to /country/CH for the handful of Swiss records, or drop the country line to map both.

examples.title: 🌳 The owl family tree (graph)
examples.tip:
The taxonomy rendered as a NODE-LINK graph — switch Output to Graph. rdfs:subClassOf+ gathers everything under the owl family Strigidae, then the CONSTRUCT rebuilds the tree: family → genera (Athene, Asio, Bubo, Strix, Otus …) → species. A living picture of a clade, all from the T-Box.
Swap /family/Strigidae for /order/Anseriformes (a bigger tree), /family/Accipitridae (hawks & eagles), or any taxon node.

datasets.label: worldcup.rete — FIFA World Cup 2022: stats, player careers & multi-source predictions (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The 2022 FIFA World Cup as one queryable knowledge graph, weaving together three things you rarely see in the same place. STATS: all 64 matches (group + full knockout) with scores, penalty shootouts, ~170 goals and their scorers, 8 stadiums with coordinates, and the final standings — Argentina champions, France runners-up. PLAYER EVOLUTION: club-by-club career timelines with start/end years (linked to Wikidata) for the marquee players, so you can trace Messi from Newell's Old Boys to Inter Miami. PREDICTIONS: what different forecasters said would happen, as timestamped, source-attributed claims — FiveThirtyEight's SPI model across 6 snapshots (pre-tournament through the quarter-finals, so you can watch Argentina's title probability dip after the shock Saudi Arabia loss and climb back), plus pre-tournament bookmaker and Opta champion odds. Each prediction is an n-ary node carrying probability + source (PROV-O) + forecast date, so you can compare parties, track how the odds moved, and score who called it best against the real result. Modelled with schema.org + Dublin Core + GeoSPARQL + a small wc: vocab on w3id.org/rete. Open data (OpenFootball, FiveThirtyEight CC-BY, Wikidata CC0).

datasets.label: tracking.rete — a full match as a spatiotemporal graph (player + ball 2D positions over time)
datasets.description: A full football match as a SPATIOTEMPORAL graph: the 2D position of every player and the ball, ~5 frames/second across ~94 minutes, on a 105x68 m pitch — 2.55M triples, ~637k position rows. From Metrica Sports' open sample data (anonymised). Each position carries tr:t (seconds), tr:x, tr:y and tr:object, so you can query any object's location in any time window — the basis for a 2D movement replay (a query returns a frame; interpolate between frames to animate). PREFIX tr: <https://w3id.org/rete/tracking#>
SELECT ("positions" AS ?metric) (COUNT(?p) AS ?n) WHERE { ?p tr:t ?t }

examples.title: 📸 Everyone's position at one instant

PREFIX tr: <https://w3id.org/rete/tracking#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?obj ?x ?y WHERE {
  ?p tr:t ?t ; tr:object ?o ; tr:x ?x ; tr:y ?y .
  ?o rdfs:label ?obj .
  FILTER(?t >= 300 && ?t < 300.2)
} ORDER BY ?obj

datasets.label: subtitles.rete — one film, 20 languages, over time (Tears of Steel · CC-BY)
datasets.description: Tears of Steel — the Blender Foundation's open sci-fi short — subtitled in TWENTY languages, as one temporal + multilingual knowledge graph (14,376 triples). It's the 'over time' idea applied to language. Every su:Line is a MOMENT in the film (su:start / su:end in seconds) carrying the SAME utterance in all 20 tongues as language-tagged literals: English, Spanish, German, French, Italian, Dutch, Russian, Polish, Czech, Hungarian, Greek, Portuguese (BR), Danish, Indonesian, Norwegian, Japanese, Chinese (Simplified + Traditional), and right-to-left Persian & Hebrew. Each su:Cue is one language track's own timed segment (its real start/end + su:text "…"@lang), aligned to the English original by time-overlap — 1,536 cues over 76 lines. So you can scrub a timeline and watch the dialogue appear in every language at once, ask 'what's on screen at 1:05 in Japanese and Persian', diff how one line was rendered across 20 cultures, or full-text-search the dialogue (a TEXT_INDEX is baked in). Subtitles are all timed to the same audio, so the shared timeline IS the cross-language alignment. Open data: Tears of Steel (CC BY 3.0, Blender Foundation, mango.blender.org), subtitle .srt files from media.xiph.org/mango. su: vocab + schema.org + Dublin Core on w3id.org/rete.

examples.title: The 20 language tracks
examples.tip:
What's in the graph: 20 subtitle tracks for one film, each a full language version. English (en) is the pivot with 76 cues; other tongues merge or split lines slightly, so counts differ.
Each track is a su:SubtitleTrack of Tears of Steel (Blender, CC BY 3.0).

examples.title: 🌍 One line, every language
examples.tip:
The film's first spoken line — “You're a jerk, Thom.” at 0:23 — in every language at once, including right-to-left Persian & Hebrew and CJK Japanese/Chinese.

examples.title: 🎬 The whole film in one language
examples.tip:
Play one language's subtitle track in order — here Japanese (ja), each su:Cue with its own start time. This is the film as a timeline of text.
Change "ja" to es, fr, ru, fa, zh-Hant … to switch language.

examples.title: ⏱ What's on screen at 1:05
examples.tip:
Freeze the film at t = 65 s (1:05) and read the line whose [su:start, su:end] interval covers that instant — in six languages side by side.
It's a time-window query: change 65 to any second to scrub the whole film.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX su: <https://w3id.org/rete/subtitles#>
SELECT ?language ?text WHERE {
  ?line a su:Line ; su:start ?s ; su:end ?e ; su:text ?text .
  FILTER(?s <= 65 && ?e >= 65)
  BIND(LANG(?text) AS ?language)
  FILTER(?language IN ("en","es","ja","ru","fa","zh-Hans"))
} ORDER BY ?language

examples.title: 🔤 Find a word in the dialogue
examples.tip:

examples.title: 🔀 How one line was translated
examples.tip:

examples.sparql:
PREFIX su: <https://w3id.org/rete/subtitles#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?time ?english (GROUP_CONCAT(CONCAT(?lg,"=",?tx); separator="   ·   ") AS ?translations) WHERE {
  ?line a su:Line ; su:start ?time ; rdfs:label ?english ; su:text ?tx .
  BIND(LANG(?tx) AS ?lg)
  FILTER(?lg IN ("es","fr","de","ru","ja"))
} GROUP BY ?line ?time ?english ORDER BY ?time LIMIT 12

datasets.label: mtg.rete — Magic: The Gathering: the whole card pool as a graph (34,633 cards, with images)
datasets.description: The entire Magic: The Gathering card pool as a queryable knowledge graph — 34,633 unique cards (Oracle-level concepts, from MTGJSON's AtomicCards, MIT-licensed) richly interlinked with their colors, card types, subtypes, keywords, mana, formats and named+dated sets, each carrying its Scryfall card IMAGE, full Oracle text and official rulings (76,990 of them). Card types are OWL classes (Creature, Instant, Sorcery, Land, Artifact, Enchantment, Planeswalker … rdfs:subClassOf mtg:Card) and every card rdf:type its types, so the Schema tab is a card-type zoom and the reasoner has a real TBox. Oracle text lives in a TEXT_INDEX, so you can find cards by what they DO ('draw two cards', 'destroy target creature'). Ask for red creatures with flying legal in Modern (and see the cards), every Goblin or Dragon ranked by EDHREC popularity, the colour pie, legendary planeswalkers, cards on the Reserved List, or what a set contains. This is the card-semantics layer from the semantic-MTG-engine plan (building on cmdoret/mtg_ontology): the executable rules engine is a separate deterministic system, but the cards ARE a graph — a big, fun, richly-joined one. mtg: vocab on w3id.org/rete + schema.org; card data MIT (MTGJSON), images © Wizards of the Coast served via Scryfall's CDN. Cyril Matthey-Doret's mtg_ontology is merged in as the TBox foundation — each card type is owl:equivalentClass its class in his ontology, and colours/keywords link to his concepts, so you can query the cards THROUGH his vocabulary.

PREFIX mtg: <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>

SELECT ?card ?ruling WHERE {

  ?r rdfs:comment ?ruling .
  FILTER(CONTAINS(LCASE(?ruling), "legend rule"))
} LIMIT 20

cmdoret/mtg_ontology is merged in as the TBox: this asks for creatures via HIS class (cmdoret:Creature), reached through owl:equivalentClass back to our mtg:Creature — the two vocabularies are one graph.

PREFIX mtg: <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>

SELECT ?image ?card WHERE {

} ORDER BY ?rank LIMIT 24

datasets.label: mtg-game.rete — a live Magic game state as OWL + SPARQL (no engine)
datasets.description: The DECLARATIVE half of the semantic-MTG-engine plan, in miniature: a runtime OWL ontology (GameState, Player, Zone, ZoneMembership, CardInstance, SpellInstance, the Stack), a handful of cards modelled with their real STRUCTURED abilities (cost / condition / effect / action — the way cmdoret/mtg_ontology intends, e.g. Bonders' Enclave's “{3},{T}: draw a card, only if you control a creature with power ≥ 4”), and one concrete match — Alice vs Bob — captured as two immutable snapshots: state S1 (Alice's turn 3, main phase) and its successor S2 after she casts Lightning Bolt at Bob's Grizzly Bears (the spell now sits on the stack, a Mountain is tapped). There is NO game engine here — just OWL classes and data — yet plain SPARQL answers the plan's question families: DESCRIBE the board, VALIDATE that every card instance is in exactly one zone, decide LEGALITY (which instants Alice can actually pay for from her untapped lands), read what each card DOES from its ability structure, and diff S1→S2. Card concepts reuse the 34k-catalogue IRIs (the `mtg` dataset), so the two graphs are one entity space. mtgg: runtime vocab on w3id.org/rete, building on Cyril Matthey-Doret's mtg_ontology (mtgo: structural classes + MTG-wiki action classes). CC BY 4.0. Its companion `mtg` is the whole card pool; this is one match modelled in full.

examples.title: 🎲 What's on the battlefield (state S1)
examples.tip:
The plan's 'Describe' question, in SPARQL: every card instance on the battlefield in game state S1 and who controls it — Alice has Llanowar Elves + two Mountains, Bob has Grizzly Bears + Serra Angel.
ZoneMembership is state-scoped, so change s1 to s2 to see the board a move later.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX mtgg: <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?controller ?card WHERE {
  ?m a mtgg:ZoneMembership ; mtgg:inState <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game/s1> ; mtgg:object ?i ; mtgg:zone <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game/battlefield> .
  ?i mtgg:ofCard ?c ; mtgg:controller ?ctrl .
  ?c schema:name ?card . ?ctrl rdfs:label ?controller .
} ORDER BY ?controller ?card

examples.title: 📜 What does each card DO?
examples.tip:
Cards aren't text blobs here — each ability is a structured object (cost / condition / effect / action), the way cmdoret/mtg_ontology models them. The action links to the MTG-wiki concept (draw, add_mana …).
Bonders' Enclave shows two abilities incl. its power-≥4 condition.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX mtgg: <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game#>
PREFIX mtg: <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?card ?ability ?action WHERE {
  ?c a mtg:Card ; schema:name ?card ; mtgg:ability ?ab .
  ?ab rdfs:label ?ability ; mtgg:effect ?e . ?e mtgg:action ?action .
} ORDER BY ?card

examples.title: ✅ Which instants can Alice cast now?
examples.tip:
The plan's 'Legality' question answered WITHOUT an engine: an instant in Alice's hand whose mana value she can pay from her untapped mana sources in S1. Lightning Bolt (cost 1) is castable — she has 2 untapped Mountains.
Tap a Mountain (use s2) and re-run to watch it drop out.

examples.title: 🧪 Is the state coherent? (one zone per card)
examples.tip:
A SHACL-style coherence check as SPARQL: every card instance must be in exactly one zone in a state. This returns the OFFENDERS — an empty result means S1 is valid.
A well-formed game state should always answer nothing here.

examples.title: 🪄 On the stack: Bolt → Bears (state S2)
examples.tip:
State S2 is the successor of S1 after Alice casts Lightning Bolt at Bob's Grizzly Bears — the spell instance now sits on the Stack with its target and controller. Successor states link back with mtgg:previousState.
This is a transition captured as data, not run by an engine.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX mtgg: <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?spell ?targetCard ?controller WHERE {
  ?m mtgg:inState <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game/s2> ; mtgg:object ?sp ; mtgg:zone <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game/stack> .
  ?sp rdfs:label ?spell ; mtgg:target ?t ; mtgg:controller ?ctrl .
  ?t mtgg:ofCard ?tc . ?tc schema:name ?targetCard . ?ctrl rdfs:label ?controller .
}

examples.title: 🔁 What changed from S1 to S2
examples.tip:
Diff two snapshots: permanents that were untapped in S1 but tapped in S2 — i.e. what paying for the Bolt cost. Here it's the one Mountain Alice tapped for {R}.
Comparing states is just a join across two mtgg:inState values.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX mtgg: <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
SELECT ?card WHERE {
  ?m2 mtgg:inState <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game/s2> ; mtgg:object ?o ; mtgg:tapped true .
  ?m1 mtgg:inState <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game/s1> ; mtgg:object ?o ; mtgg:tapped false .
  ?o mtgg:ofCard ?c . ?c schema:name ?card .
}

datasets.label: arxiu.rete — Arxius en Línia: complete Catalan archives, with scanned documents
datasets.description: Complete Catalan archives from the Generalitat de Catalunya's online archives (Arxius en Línia), harvested one whole archive at a time and merged into a single graph. Four complete archives so far — the Arxiu Nacional de Catalunya (431,776 units), the Arxiu Comarcal de l'Anoia (137,054), the Arxiu Comarcal del Baix Llobregat (53,644) and the Arxiu Històric de Tarragona (7,401) — 629,875 archival units across 507 fonds. Each archival unit carries its holding archive, fonds, reference code, dates, description AND its scanned document: non-reserved scans are shown as a downsized WebP (~180 KB, ~15% of the ~1.5 MB original) mirrored to R2 so they render inline in query results, and every unit keeps arx:originalImage → the original full-res JPEG on Gencat's own server (the source of record). Reserved documents — 56% of Tarragona, 93% of Baix Llobregat, 99% of Anoia, 73% of the ANC — keep only the link, respecting the holding archives' rights (so ~117,940 units render a WebP — photographs plus PDF documents shown by their rendered first page; the rest are metadata + the original Gencat link). The same open API holds ~1.43M image-records across ~65 archives (~1.5 TB); this graph grows archive by archive. Modelled with schema.org archival vocabulary (schema:ArchiveComponent held by an ArchiveOrganization, part of a Collection/fonds) on w3id.org/rete. Descriptions are openly reusable (Llicència oberta d'ús d'informació / Llei 37/2007, Generalitat de Catalunya, with attribution).

datasets.label: zenodo-records.rete — every Zenodo record (7.76M) as a DataCite scholarly graph (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: Every published record on Zenodo — CERN's open research repository — as one 215M-triple range-queryable graph (2.09 GB, remote-lazy over HTTP range on Cloudflare R2). Built from the OFFICIAL Zenodo exporter dump (the site-wide records-xml snapshot: 7,759,325 records, each DataCite kernel-4.5 metadata) — essentially ALL of Zenodo's descriptive metadata: datasets, software, preprints, journal articles, images, presentations, theses… Each record sits at its CANONICAL DOI IRI (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8435696) and is typed both zen:Record and its DataCite resource class (dcite:Dataset, dcite:Software, dcite:JournalArticle, dcite:Image, dcite:Preprint …) — so the type-pyramid communities ARE the kinds of research output: JournalArticle 2.41M, Text 1.40M, Image 1.23M, Dataset 875k, Software 645k. It carries dcite:title, dcite:publisherName, dcite:publicationYear, dcite:landingPage, the license, dcterms:subject keywords, and — the connective tissue — the DataCite RELATION NETWORK mined from relatedIdentifiers: dcite:isVersionOf (every version → its concept DOI), dcite:isPartOf, dcite:cites / dcite:references / dcite:isSupplementTo, mapped as edges between DOIs so version chains and citation/derivation links are all traversable. 877,926 CREATOR nodes carry an ORCID and mint at their canonical https://orcid.org/{orcid} IRI. Because works are keyed by DOI and people by ORCID, this graph AUTO-MERGES with the DataCite / OpenAIRE / OpenCitations / ORCID / DBLP scholarly datasets on the shared identifiers — the same node, no owl:sameAs (see data/scholar/scholar.ttl). Built by scripts/zenodo/records_to_nt.py (Parquet → N-Triples honoring the scholar-alignment canonical-IRI policy) → rete build --pyramid-algo types --card. CC-BY 4.0 (Zenodo metadata export). Selective queries — one DOI's neighbourhood, an author's works, a keyword — are cheap over HTTP range; a full 215M-triple aggregate scans the file, so lean on the Schema pyramid for the big picture.

examples.tip:

datasets.label: biosyslit.rete — Zenodo Biodiversity Literature Repository: taxonomic treatments with Darwin Core taxonomy + IIIF (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The Biodiversity Literature Repository (BLR) community on Zenodo — curated by Plazi / Pensoft — as one 106M-triple range-queryable graph (1.65 GB, remote-lazy over HTTP range). 2,013,749 records, of which 688,222 are TAXONOMIC TREATMENTS (zen:TaxonomicTreatment ⊑ dcite:Text): each describes a taxon and carries the full DARWIN CORE taxonomy directly in the dwc: namespace — dwc:kingdom / dwc:phylum / dwc:class / dwc:order / dwc:family / dwc:genus, dwc:taxonRank, dwc:scientificNameAuthorship — so you can roll treatments up by family (Staphylinidae 17,101, Formicidae 15,424, Cerambycidae 12,068, Ichneumonidae, Curculionidae…), order or genus WITHOUT touching a single record. Every record sits at its canonical DOI IRI and carries dcite:title, the full treatment description text, usage stats (zen:views / zen:downloads), an IIIF manifest (zen:iiifManifest → the treatment's figures on Zenodo's IIIF server), its files (zen:hasFile → treatment.html / images with mime + byte size) and its community membership (zen:inCommunity → the biosyslit zen:Community node). The RELATION NETWORK links each treatment to its source journal article and related treatments (dcite:isPartOf / dcite:cites / dcite:isVersionOf → other DOIs). Because works are DOIs and ORCID authors mint at orcid.org, it federates with the DataCite / OpenAIRE / ORCID scholarly graph — and it is a rich subset of the sibling `zenodo-records` graph (BLR records ARE Zenodo records), kept separate for the Zenodo-native detail (IIIF, files, Darwin Core) that the bare DataCite metadata drops. Built by scripts/zenodo/biosyslit_to_nt.py → rete build --pyramid-algo types --card. CC-BY 4.0. The richest slice of Zenodo for biodiversity.

datasets.label: gotriple.rete — GoTriple: 2.7M Social-Sciences & Humanities publications, DOI-federated (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The GoTriple metadata corpus — the EU-funded discovery platform for the Social Sciences & Humanities (gotriple.eu / TRIPLE / OPERAS) — as one 57.7M-triple range-queryable graph (832 MB, remote-lazy over HTTP range on Cloudflare R2). Built from the CC0 Zenodo dump (18185971): 6,074,813 discipline-placements that DEDUPLICATE, under rete's canonical-IRI policy, into 2,712,267 DISTINCT publications — a multi-disciplinary paper (same GoTriple id across several discipline files) and a paper indexed from several providers (same DOI) MERGE into one gtr:Document node that carries all its gtr:inDiscipline tags (so 855,688 distinct DOIs come from 2.46M DOI-bearing records, ~2.9 copies each). Each document carries a multilingual gtr:title, its GoTriple discipline(s) (a 26-term SKOS scheme: History, Sociology, Law, Psychology, Economics, Linguistics, Philosophy, Art…), authors, keywords, source provider/publisher, language, access status and its full-text URL — and, the connective tissue, gtr:knowsAbout → shared SSH-LCSH subject-authority nodes (semantics.gr, with multilingual labels) that DEDUPE across the whole corpus into a real subject graph (Education links 288k docs, Economics 229k, 'State, The' 219k…). The 855,688 documents WITH a DOI mint at their canonical https://doi.org/{doi} IRI, so this graph AUTO-MERGES with the DataCite / Zenodo / OpenAIRE / OpenCitations scholarly datasets on the shared DOI — and it brings the SSH breadth those STEM-heavy sources lack (see data/scholar/scholar.ttl). The go-triple.ttl ontology (gtr:) travels INSIDE the file. Built by scripts/gotriple/{jsonl_to_parquet,gotriple_to_nt}.py → rete build --no-pyramid + rete repyramid --pyramid-algo types. CC0. Selective queries — one DOI, a subject's documents, an open-access slice of one discipline — are cheap over HTTP range; a full-corpus aggregate scans the file, so lean on the Schema pyramid for the big picture.
